Heading: The dangers of being the same - Indian Express
Content:
Seema Chishti is right in thinking that the belief of the ruling alliance that any tough action against "criminals behind bomb blasts" is in conflict with secularism is "the most 'communal' thought to have'. They are speaking with conflicting voices: some voices have started urging a tougher anti-terrorist law, others are opposing it. Hence, efforts to go after terrorists lose urgency.

—M. Ratan

New Delhi

Regulation failure

This is with reference to the editorial 'In difficult times'. In the series of failures culminating in Lehman's collapse, one brutal fact emerges: the crisis has its roots in the lack of regulation in the US economy. Risk assessment was totally absent when the funds were dispensed to the customers. More importantly multiple packaging and securitising of these assets further hid the risks underneath. And when things became clear the crisis had covered the whole market. US may be trying to save these entities but they are a severe blow to the advocates of accelerated financial reforms. India must learn the proper lesson from the current situation.

—Ashwani Sharma

Ghaziabad

Report problems

I read your editorial 'Laws and agencies'. Whatever the flaws in the present security laws are, the main causes of our failure to tackle terrorism are: the ineptitude of our political leadership in the states and at the Centre, its undue interference in the working of the state and central security and intelligence agencies and lack of coordination among them.

The debate on security reforms which started with the submission of a report by Veerappa Moily is a welcome step but the government may use it to deflect public criticism from its dismal failure on controlling terror.

—Tarsem Singh

New Delhi

Cheeky Sangh

This refers to your edit "Is this Karnataka?". The cohorts of the BJP slap a minority population in Orissa for whatever reason, and when the victims shut down minority institutions in protest, the party has no compunctions in slapping them again, on the other cheek, in Karnataka. A case of the devil quoting the scriptures in reverse. And, ironically, they do this while raising a hue and cry over the lack of deterrent laws against acts of terror.

—R. Narayanan Ghaziabad

No more

It's time to say "enough is enough". We all know what the terrorists' agenda is — to kill and create panic. But do they have a real grievance against the nation? With the random killings we have seen, it doesn't seem so. All Indians just want to live in peace and harmony and get on with their lives. All we can hope is that the security agencies get more proactive than they are right now and nab the real terrorists who perpetrate such crimes.

—Farzana Nigar

Ranchi

Heading: Blame it on Ma - Indian Express
Content:
Georgian and Russian societies are remarkably similar. In both countries, we see the desire to rally the people around the state regardless of their leaders' faults and mistakes. They both also believe that the state should hold onto its separatist territories at all costs... but there is one fundamental difference between public opinion in Georgia and Russia. In Georgia, nationalism is pervasive, and the few who might feel differently are careful to remain silent. In Russia, dissenting voices can always be heard, even when patriotic fervour reaches unprecedented levels...

When a small state dominated by a single ethnic group whips up nationalistic sentiment, it has an amazing power to mobilise the entire community in support of a single idea or belief, leaving almost no room for criticism. During the Soviet era, the Moscow intelligentsia took a patronising pleasure in the ethnic solidarity among people from the Baltic states — particularly when it was compared to the lack of unification among ethnic Russians. Many Russians admired the Baltic song festivals, in which thousands of people lined up in long columns. But the scenes always made me uneasy because of their striking resemblance to the mass rallies of Hitler's Third Reich.

Georgia is far from being the only former Soviet republic with a uniform public opinion. You would have trouble finding anyone in Armenia who could understand Azerbaijan's position regarding the conflict in Nagorno-Karabakh. Many contemporary Turkish intellectuals would willingly risk going to jail for stating that almost 100 years ago, a genocide of Armenian citizens did, in fact, occur on Turkish soil, even though the Turkish government denies it. But I do not know of a single Armenian intellectual who has ever written anything that treats Turkish history and culture with respect...

Paradoxically, the split in Russian public opinion between supporters and opponents of the country's imperial traditions is far more similar to public sentiment in Western Europe than to many countries on Russia's borders.

Extracted from a comment by Boris Kagarlitsky in 'The Moscow Times'

Heading: Failing Tests, repeatedly - Indian Express
Content:
Last night, I was reading an article about how all of India is now talking about sex. On radio shows, in columns, there's been a revolution of sorts; people want to be more informed about sex. I remembered the time I first came across the Word. Back in the early '90s, I spent a summer glued to MTV and learning the lyrics of Salt'n'Pepa's Let's talk about sex. The last word was unknown to me and so I asked my mother, "Ma, what is sex?" in my best child-is-innocently-curious voice.

She was brushing her hair, she stopped when she heard me. I was five years old — I'm surprised she didn't have a heart attack. She looked into the mirror and asked me to return in five minutes, knowing perfectly well that if she didn't come up with an answer, I would ask everyone around the same question. To prevent mass heart failure, five minutes later, she answered carefully, "Sex is Love." I nodded, I knew I had learnt an important word today.

That evening, I went down to play with my best friends, Joanne, her brother Andrew and Bunny. Bunny had a huge crush on Jo and he agreed with everything she said. So in my bid to outdo Jo that day, I went up to her and asked "Joanne, do you sex your mom?" Joanne looked stunned, this was a new word she didn't know and she couldn't afford to look stupid in front of Bunny. Feeling more confident, I continued to ask questions. That was it, Joanna said "What does sex mean?"

I stood there, took my time, looked at my sneakers before I slowly looked up and said calmly, "Love. It means Love."

I taught them the lyrics to the Salt'n'Pepa song and we sang it, loudly, in front of many scandalised neighbours.

A week after that, at a party, a woman raised the issue saying "I don't know what has happened to the kids. That day, I saw these four kids and they were screaming a song about sex something... haw... Mrs Majumdar, can you believe it?" My mother took another sip from her glass and replied, "I wonder where they picked it up."

Heading: Fear factor - Indian Express
Content:
Over the last week, the Indian Cricket League (ICL) has suddenly sprung out of a grave by unveiling the Dhaka Warriors, a team comprising of current and former Bangladesh players, the biggest coup in its brief history. And the International Cricket Council (ICC), as usual, is silently watching the drama unfold.

It's hard to put a finger right away on how much difference the ICL announcement will actually make to world cricket, or even Bangladesh cricket, especially in the short term. Just over a year ago, they beat both India and South Africa at the world cup in the Caribbean, and followed that up by beating the West Indies in the Twenty20 world championship. But had they finally arrived?

Of the 53 games they have played since making their Test debut in November 2000, they have lost 47, drawn five and won a grand total of one — and that against a spiralling Zimbabwe more than three years ago. Their last two Tests they lost at home to South Africa by an innings and 205 runs and an innings and 324 runs.

It was hard to imagine things getting any worse. Until now.

Bangladesh might find seven replacements for the seven contracted rebels. But who's to say there won't be another bunch of players, disgruntled with meagre pay packets and tired of losing day in and day out, leaving for greener pastures 12 months from now?

There were calls, four years ago, to revoke Bangladesh's Test status; the argument was that they had been pushed up too early by Jagmohan Dalmiya for an extra vote in the bag in his many battles against the International Cricket Council. But the ICC, which talks incessantly about spreading the game far and wide, couldn't afford to lose a Test-playing nation then. And with Zimbabwe already out, they definitely can't now.

The funny thing is that the lack of reaction from Dubai has been predictable. In recent times, any issue with any kind of relevance to the present or future of the game has been met with deafening silence from the men who run the ICC.

Pakistan vs. England at The Oval in 2006, the first forfeited Test in the history of cricket. Exactly 23 months later, the forfeiture is overturned to a draw. For prompt action, trust the ICC.

The UK government cut all ties with Robert Mugabe's Zimbabwe, putting England, the hosts of the 2009 T20 world cup, in a spot. The ICC wait, and wait some more, until Zimbabwe themselves offer to not travel to England, and not play Test cricket until things got better back home.

The racism row in Australia this year — an issue that international sport takes extremely seriously — was left to the Indian and Australian boards to sort out. If you ignore a problem for long enough, it disappears. Hopefully.

Pakistan were scheduled to host the Champions Trophy this month, but for over a month-and-a-half, at least four major teams expressed unwillingness to travel there. The ICC, predictably, let things be long enough that alternate venues were not an option. So they postponed it by a year, keeping the tournament in Pakistan. What if Australia, South Africa, England and New Zealand still refuse to travel 12 months down the line? They'll probably wait and watch when they come to that bridge.

In fact, the ICC hasn't even termed the ICL a rebel league yet. Their lawyers recommended, a few months ago, changes in their constitution that would confirm ICL's rebel status, but no action has yet been taken.

The international body's defence is that it's only a collection of the member boards and that any decision it takes — or doesn't take, as is more often the case — is collective.

What are its powers then? What is its purpose? To organise a glittering awards function once a year? To prepare Future Tours Programmes which are too crammed anyway? To spread the game to Beijing and New York, even as Dhaka and Harare struggle to survive?

Going by recent history, this is probably how things will pan out: Bangladesh will keep losing Test matches and pull off the occasional one-day upset — less regularly, perhaps, than they did in the past. But then, that's the Bangladesh Cricket Board's problem, not the ICC's. Finally, perhaps, Bangladesh will themselves say they'll stop playing Test cricket until they're ready once again.

It's not even playing with a straight bat; the ICC just keep letting balls go until one darts back in to knock them over.

deepak.narayanan@expressindia.com

Heading: 20,000 MW politics - Indian Express
Content:
There's plenty of we-told-you-so and some glee among many members of the Indian establishment following the US financial crisis. This will now almost certainly translate into resistance against any medium or big financial liberalisation measure. Logic won't matter; what will is a supposed contrast between high risk-loving Wall Street managers and India's safe haven status. But let's look at the logic anyway. It is necessary and inevitable that there will be changes in the US and Western financial system after this crisis. But we must surely see that we are in a different planet — our underdeveloped financial system should be still asking how we can extend banking to millions more people, deepen the pathetically shallow market for debt instruments, add more financial instruments. These are taken for granted in the West, which is asking questions of a different level of sophistication. We should study those questions and the future answers. But India's priorities have hardly changed dramatically because Lehman went bankrupt.

Let's also remember that everyone, well almost everyone, wants India to grow. Financial reform sceptics who are growth champions should admit that sophisticated finance is part of the toolkit of high growth. India simply cannot grow fast continuously with not even 50 major banks — the largest of which is puny by international comparisons — and a small financial system. The really sad thing about this false thesis is that some of the finest intellectual material for financial reform is available now; there are three or four politicans in the ruling party, beginning with the prime minister, who understand the need for liberal finance; there's even a different dispensation at the RBI. Wall Street chose a bad time as far as India is considered to display the results of its over-exuberant betting.

So nothing will happen? Maybe some politically undramatic but financially significant changes can be effected. The Rajan committee's suggestion on universalising bank accounts should be politically welcomed. Some reform on debt management is possible because it's a technical issue and the RBI now should be more receptive to it. Perhaps, pressure of growth will liberalise the permit raj on allowing new banks. Everything else will be on hold.

Heading: Window in the east - Indian Express
Content:
The economics section of the post-nuclear deal narrative seems to have been written already: orders will flow and Indian and foreign engineering firms will make money. This is not wrong. But it's terribly unambitious. The nuclear deal can be a domestic reform accelerator.

To see this, consider the basic objective: increasing nuclear power generation. The most quoted forecast is 20,000 megawatt (MW) by 2020. For power production, the crucial calculation is cost per MW. Thanks to pre-nuclear deal import restrictions and therefore fully indigenous engineering, nuclear power in India is costly — Rs 8 crore to Rs 9 crore per MW. With India re-entering global nuclear commerce, costs can come down. But there's a countervailing factor: the price of better technology.

Nuclear power has a high capital cost/low operating cost characteristic. That means time overruns are very expensive. One way to quickly construct nuclear power plants is via standardised design — the same model is replicated across plants. France has done this with great success.

Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd (NPCIL), the state-owned agency that designs, constructs, commissions and operates nuclear power plants, says its expertise in building standardised, no-time delay 220 MW nuclear power plants is proven. But the 220 MW size is small and inefficient in the nuclear power business. NPCIL runs 15 small-sized reactors and 2 medium-sized ones. There are six under construction, of which two are 1,000 MW size.

France's nuclear power programme relies on large plants, 1,300 MW to 1,450 MW. There's nothing of this size Indian technology can build now. The 1,000 MW plants in India are being built by Russian technology. The French are better at this; Americans incidentally are not the world leaders in this field. So for India to get the best out of the nuclear deal, it must import the best technology for standardised, large plants.

Now, NPCIL can still be in charge of this import-led project, provided the government can find the money. One estimate of the cost of nuclear power produced with the best technology, quoted by The Economist among others, is $2,000 per kilowatt (KW). That works out to Rs 9 crore per MW (1 MW is 1,000 KW, and $1 is 45 rupees). But since India will import the technology one should add charges like transport, installation and service. Sudha Mahalingam, who writes on energy and is with the Nehru Memorial Museum and Library, has put a figure of Rs 10 crore per MW for best practice nuclear power generation in India.

Simple arithmetic tells us 20,000 MW at Rs 10 crore per MW means an investment of Rs 200,000 crore. If the government has to be in charge of producing nuclear power, it has to find this money. Let's relax the 2020 deadline and say India must produce 20,000 MW of nuclear power in 20 years. Even that means an official commitment of Rs 10,000 crore every year for 20 years for just one source of power — there are thermal, hydro, naptha, etc. The Centre currently spends around Rs 28,000 crore every year on the entire power sector. Even minimum familiarity with the government's fiscal ability will tell anyone that this order of official financial commitment for one segment of the power sector is unrealistic.

Ergo, let the private sector in to produce nuclear power, amend the Atomic Energy Act. Job done? Not quite. There are, as commentators like Mahalingam argue, problems. But actually, those problems are opportunities. Our argument is that, given the enormous political prestige attached to nuclear power, creating the policy infrastructure for supporting huge private sector investment can be accelerated as never before.

India's efforts to attract private investment in power have been sabotaged by the bankruptcy of power buyers — state electricity boards (SEBs), which purchase power and transmit and distribute it or transmit it to private distributors. If you want to commit a large amount of money in a power project you would not want your buyers to be bankrupt. This problem has been dealt with in typical Indian fashion since the mid-'90s — ad hoc solutions, poor results. One good recent idea has been open access, allowing power producers to sell directly to distributors and to consumers. Right now, consumers with more than 1 MW of power requirement can be open access buyers.

This has already energised investment in hydropower. Reliance, GMR, Lanco, Jaiprakash Industries, etc have hydropower projects in Arunachal Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Open access means a hydropower producer in Himachal Pradesh can sell to industrial consumers in Maharashtra. Private backers of hugely capital intensive nuclear power require exactly this kind of incentive. Open access reform can therefore get supercharged by the needs of nuclear plants.

Nuclear power can also help reform power tariffs, which are government-determined and uneconomical. They are one reason SEBs are bankrupt. The market, with a regulator watching, should set tariffs. Nuclear power's commercial attractiveness comes from the fact of its low operating costs. If tariffs are economic, nuclear power producers look at better profit margins than thermal power producers; this is necessary because, remember, nuclear power has bigger capital costs. Therefore high profile, politically prestigious nuclear power projects can put more pressure on tariff reform than anything else has done so far.

The same with another, even more contentious reform agenda: land for industry. Singur will be small beer compared to land required for a series of nuclear power projects. Safety considerations mean land buying for nuclear power plants will be more complicated. Government nuclear power projects, until the Kalpakkam plant was built, never used to bother with local considerations. More than NGOs, reformists should object to this.

Land for projects is necessary but is a complex subject. With private sector nuclear power producers, local interrogation and NGO activity will be intense — the Koondakulam plant under construction has already seen this — because anything nuclear attracts extra questions. Given the immensely high political stakes riding on the nuclear power programme, a lot of political capital will be devoted to finding creative land for industry formulas.

India reforms quickly under extraordinary circumstances (think the payments crisis of 1990). The prospect of the hard-won, global profile enhancing nuclear deal failing at home due to bad policy is an extraordinary circumstance. Pakistan will laugh. China will smirk. The world will wonder. Political prestige will take a huge blow.

Politicians therefore will have a great incentive to reform.

saubhik.chakrabarti@expressindia.com

Heading: More teaching aids, brightly done up govt schools attract students - Indian Express
Content:
Prosecutors in an Italian court Thursday asked the key middleman in the IAF's VVIP chopper deal whether the initials 'AP' in an alleged "budget sheet" for bribes to politicians referred to Ahmed Patel, the political secretary of UPA chairperson Sonia Gandhi.

The middleman, Guido Haschke, who has consistently denied bribing Indian officials or politicians, replied that he did not know who or what 'AP' stood for.

As first reported by The Indian Express, Italian prosecutors had last month produced a handwritten document they alleged was a "budget" drawn up by two middlemen — Haschke and Christian Michel — which purportedly lists initials of Indian politicians and designations of bureaucrats and IAF officers who allegedly had to be "handled" to fix the Rs 3,546 crore deal.

The alleged "budget sheet" detailed how kickbacks of 51 million euros would be divided and under the heading "POL" — Haschke has claimed this referred to Indian politicians — there is a reference to "AP" against which "3 million euro" has been listed.

Another amount of 15/16 million euros was listed against "FAM" which is said to be "Family". Haschke has claimed the note was dictated to him by British consultant Michel during one of their meetings in 2008.

On Thursday, Italian prosecutor Eugenio Fusco asked Haschke during a court hearing in Busto Arsizio near Milan whether "AP" in the note was a reference to Ahmed Patel.

In his reply, the middlemen said he did not know what AP meant when he wrote it down. Haschke also denied any bribes were paid for the contract and said that the "budget sheet" was just an imaginary note drawn up and was never acted upon.

He also said the budget sheet was merely bragging by Michel about his Indian contacts and that Haschke tried to disassociate himself from the Briton.

Strongly denying any wrongdoing in the deal, Haschke also claimed to Indian interrogators in the court that no bribes were paid for the contract and that the money he received from AgustaWestland - in excess of 24 million euros - is justified as fees for engineering consultations.

Italian prosecutors also produced another note in court Thursday - a March 2008 fax by Michel to Peter Hulett, said to be the then head of region, govt sales at AgustaWestland's India office. The fax said that among the politicians who would use the choppers once acquired by India would be UPA chairperson Sonia Gandhi and her senior advisors, including Ahmed Patel.

However, Sonia is not entitled to use government helicopters. She can use VIP aircraft only when she flies with the PM, President or ministers who are officially entitled to the aircraft. This fax by the British middleman has also been shared by the Italian side with the CBI team that is in Busto Arsizio for the hearing.

Michel has been elusive and no investigative agency has been able to reach him.

Haschke, who is facing a case in Italy for being part of a conspiracy to bribe Indian officials to ensure the AW 101 chopper was picked by the IAF, faced several questions from the Indian side and denied any irregularity.

But the Indian side did not ask Haschke to explain what AP, FAM or any of the other acronyms in the note - "DS", "JS AIR", "AFA", "DG Acquisition", CVC" etc - referred to, source said.

The middleman, who was quizzed about his association with former Air Chief S P Tyagi - named as an accused in the CBI case in the deal - denied that any money had been paid to the retired Indian officer. Haschke, sources said, admitted that he was in regular touch with three cousins of Tyagi who have also been named in the case.

In response to a question from the Indian side, Haschke said he was not aware if any money was paid to S P Tyagi.

The UPA government had come under pressure in connection with the alleged kickbacks last month after The Indian Express report on the budget sheet of the middlemen. The opposition BJP had demanded the government reveal what or who "AP" and "FAM" stand for. The party also said that it wants a detailed discussion in Parliament on "alleged payments to persons close to the ruling establishment" in connection with the controversial chopper deal and has accused the government of "running away from discussions".

The discussion did not take place as the Parliament session was abruptly called off midway.

Heading: IGNOU steps in to enable jail inmates to teach - Indian Express
Content:
The blades of a whirring fan reveal the colours of the rainbow, and a caterpillar painted on the wall displays the numberline for students to see and remember. Brightly-painted desks have measuring scales indicating width and length, and the grill on the window has different shapes in it.

Government schools in Delhi are taking rapid steps to catch up with the kind of facilities private primary schools take for granted, thanks to the Building as Learning Aid (BaLA) programme.

BaLA essentially involves using simple painting and construction work to brighten up classrooms and allow optimum utilisation of building resources.

"The Delhi Government started the programme in January 2008. We'll be giving all our schools a sum of Rs 2 lakh per annum for the implementation of BaLA," said Reena Ray, Secretary Education in the Delhi Government.

The programme is the outcome of a concept proposed by Vinyas Centre for Architectural Research and Design, and has been recommended to all states across the country.

"However, it is the Delhi government that has pioneered its implementation in schools," says OP Mishra, the Deputy Director of Education, in charge of the Vidyalaya Kalyan Samiti Programme.

"Government schools are seen as the last option, but now the cleaning, painting and other work is attracting more students," says Neeraj Rai, a class X student of the Government Boys' Senior Secondary School, Rajokri. Navayuga School, run by the New Delhi Municipal Council at Mandir Marg is one of the 'model schools' where a number of project ideas have been incorporated. The alphabet has been painted alongwith pictures on the wall in class I. All classroom doors have been painted in bright colours and pictures made on them so that when the door is opened, the picture gets divided into symmetrical halves.

Meenu Verma, headmistress of the school, said the introduction of BaLA had made it easier to keep students interested in studies.

"The paintings allow a child to improvise and develop artistic skills, and give them scope for wider thinking, instead of simple rote learning," she added.

Heading: Functioning of DPS Society: HC three-member team to look into Khurshid’s complaints - Indian Express
Content:
A jail sentence will no longer put an end to the education of the convicted. In a new initiative launched by Indira Gandhi National Open University (IGNOU), qualified inmates will be trained to teach their peers and spread their knowledge. Vice-Chancellor Rajasekharan Pillai said the system would ensure that the knowledge of inmates does not go waste.

"The inmates have been leading an aimless existence despite holding promise. We decided not to let them waste their knowledge and trained them to take up the job of teachers," the IGNOU Vice- Chancellor said. He also informed that the education programme for jail inmates would soon come free of cost.

Talking about the eligibility criteria of teachers, IGNOU Pro Vice-Chancellor Om Prakash Mishra said it would depend on availability and experience. "Any person who has qualification and experience will be able to teach according to his or her capabilities. We do not have a fixed criteria," he said.

Involving qualified inmates in imparting training to others came in quite handy at Tihar Jail in the Capital a couple of years ago when IGNOU opened a study centre. Buoyed by the success of this programme, IGNOU decided to cover jails across the country.

As many as 2,700 inmates of Tihar Jail are enrolled under IGNOU now. Inmates in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Guwahati and Karnataka are now attending classes and their enthusiasm has proved to be a catalyst for others.

Heading: CM ‘encroaches’ into Mayor’s territory, Mehra fumes - Indian Express
Content:
The Delhi High Court on Friday deputed three eminent persons, including Governor of Haryana A R Kidwai and Vice-Chairperson of Planning Commission Montek Singh Ahluwalia, to look into allegations of "irregularities" in the functioning of Delhi Public School (DPS) Society raised by its former president and senior Congress leader Salman Khurshid.

Khurshid had recently moved the Delhi High Court after the Society expelled him for objecting to the style of functioning of the latter's management.

Justice Hima Kohli, who heard the case, asked Kidwai, Ahluwalia and a leading member of the DPS Society, Sharda Nayak, to hear both sides and amicably resolve issues raised in Khurshid's petition.

The court further posted the matter for September 30. Khurshid, who challenged his expulsion order of September 1, claimed he had pointed out several irregularities in the working of the society. He alleged the society management, which runs 130 schools across the country, was illegally collecting money from its affiliated schools in the name of licence fee and signing fee, much against the norms of the Delhi Education Act.

His expulsion allegedly followed a decision to intimate in writing all the 119 affiliated schools, asking them to become full-time members of the society, Khurshid submitted.

"Instead of correcting its mistake, the society issued a letter informing that he shall cease to be a member of the DPS Society," the former Uttar Pradesh Congress Committee chief said in court.

"The issues we have raised cannot be limited to the working of a society, but affects the future of over 1.5 lakh children studying in these affiliated schools which are attractive because of the DPS tag. We are against the commercialisation of education and the court has intervened in a big way here," said Hamidullah Bhat, counsel for Khurshid.

The Congress leader had first become a member of the DPS society in 1984 and its president in 1993.

Heading: Movie reviews - Indian Express
Content:
HDIL lets its slip show: designers are paid to participate

India's first couture week is tripping on its baby steps. Not only is the show earning the brickbats of designers and media alike for its shoddy show area and poor-quality organisation, but a few designers have also let out that they were actually paid to present fashion shows here.

In fashion weeks across the globe, whether ready-to-wear or menswear, designers have to pay a participation fee. Many are rejected on other grounds as well, not enough experience, not enough selling points and the like. But to actually offer money for participation takes away from the credibility of the event and makes it an expensive but brilliant marketing gig for the sponsor company. In this case, it is the Housing Development and Infrastructure Ltd (HDIL), a real-estate development company better known for its page-three proprietor Sunny Dewan Wadhawan and his wife Anu.

The designers from Mumbai have been paid Rs 20 lakh to put up a show, while the designers from Delhi have been paid Rs 24 lakh each.

"I was paid Rs 24 lakh," says Varun Bahl, one of fashion's newest faces. "We were paid because they only gave us a structure for a stage and we had to take care of the models, choreographers, sets, hair and make-up personnel." Bahl adds that they didn't pay a participation fee at all and "for the first three years, this seems to be the structure".

The HDIL-sponsored India Couture Week is taking place in Mumbai, at the Grand Hyatt hotel, from September 16 to September 21. It has some of India's biggest designers showing their excessive and elaborate designs; the cost of an average outfit is Rs 3 lakh. Some of the invited designers are Tarun Tahiliani, JJ Valaya, Pallavi Jaikishen, Manish Malhotra, Rohit Bal, Suneet Varma and Ritu Kumar.

Even though the HDIL has tied up with the Fashion Design Council of India (FDCI), the country's official governing fashion body, for the Couture Week, the designers are hand-picked by the HDIL which has a three-year contract with the FDCI. Some names, like Jaikishen and Malhotra, are not registered with the FDCI either. "They have just registered themselves as FDCI members," corrects Sunil Sethi, the new FDCI president, "But HDIL did have an independent, anonymous jury to choose designers. Ninety per cent of these designers would have made our list anyway."

"We haven't been paid a single penny," avers Suneet Varma, who replicated the sets of his "Midsummer's Night Dream" collection he was to present on Delhi last Saturday and cancelled on account of the bombings. "The remuneration is for the production costs. Anywhere in the world, you need to be invited to take part in a couture week and you cannot just pay to get in," he adds, stating he has previously participated in couture weeks at Rome, Hong Kong, Shanghai and even Paris.

But Sumeet Nair, whose brainchild the India Couture Week was while he was still executive director of the FDCI until three months ago, had stated that the participation fee for designers would be Rs 12 lakh each.

"Since this is the first couture week, we wanted to make it larger than life where production is concerned," justifies Sethi. "Let's say, instead of taking Rs 4 crore from the sponsor ourselves, we asked them to pay the designers. Going forward, we are also going to put up a set of rules on who can be called a couture designer."

Heading: Swinging in the rain: Jyoti back in hunt - Indian Express
Content:
Welcome to Sajjanpur

CAST: Shreyas Talpade, Amrita Rao, Divya Dutta, Yashpal Sharma, Ravi Kissan, Rajeshwari Sachdev, Ila Arun

DIRECTOR: Shyam Benegal

WELCOME to the return of Shyam Benegal. The director, who's been meandering for some time with stodgy biopics and moral science lessons, is back doing what he is best at: creating life-like characters to tell life-like stories.

Sajjanpur is a modern-day, hovering-on-the-edge-of-prosperity Indian 'gaon', where 'bijli' and 'pani' have made inroads, as well as 'kutcha' roads and rattling buses. But illiteracy is still rampant. Which is why Mahadev (Shreyas), the village's only 'padha likha' young fellow, hangs up a shingle under a 'bargad' tree, and makes a living writing letters. And reading them out, also for a charge.

All kinds of people wash up under that tree: a loony aunt (Ila Arun) worrying about her 'manglik' niece (Divya), a lovelorn wife (Amrita) waiting to hear from her husband, away for four years in Bambai, a local 'neta' (Yashpal) who can easily pass off as a goon, a compounder (Ravi) in love with a pretty widow (Rajeshwari).

Welcome to Sajjanpur stays quirky and engaging even when the pace flags, and the rural accents turns faux, because of the felt screenplay and superbly robust, earthy dialogues by Ashok Mishra (this is a U/A film). The fact that the village is really a set is evident too, but you overlook it all when you see how skilfully Benegal brings up the ills that beset us still, after all these years. If a girl is unlucky, marry her off to a dog. If a eunuch stands for election, get rid of her.

But none of these 'issues' are in your face, and the film is saved from becoming the sort of dreaded preachy treatises that the director has been delivering of late. And a large part of that has to do with Shreyas Talpade, who wears his writer-of-letters-and-arbiter-of-lives role like a second skin: comforter of the lonely wife, his thoughts lead him astray, but his heart stays steadfast. But the real hero of the film is the village and the way it melds the past and the present: the profusion of all the Rams (Ram Ashrey, Ram Khilavan, Ram Singh), the references to Sita, and 'Kalyug', as well as the acknowledgment that a cell phone text message is also a letter!

The village had all but disappeared from Hindi cinema. Welcome to Sajjanpur.

Hulla

CAST: Sushant Singh, Rajat Kapoor,

Kartika Rane, Vrajesh Hirjee

DIRECTOR: Jaideep Varma

THIS is the week of the small film doing big things. Hulla, directed by debutant Jaideep Varma, is another welcome step towards getting back to celluloid centre-stage real people, real motives and real problems.

Smart broker Raj (Sushant) moves in with his wife Abha (Kartika) to a far-flung but nice suburban housing society. That's not enough for her South Mumbai parents, but she's fine till he's fine. And then one fine day, he's not. The building's night watchman whistles too loudly. Raj can't sleep. He petitions the society's self-important secretary Janardhan (Rajat) to get the fellow to stop. He acquires dark circles and a pounding head. He tries explaining his troubles to a colleague and friend (Vrajesh), to his irate boss, to a cop at the local police station, to anyone who will listen. And finds only noise.

Hulla reminds you of the middle-of-the-road cinema that lit up the 70s: it has a very Sai Paranjpye-ish feel to it. The plot's simple. But the treatment makes it a whimsical, affectionate study of people. As they are, and as they'd like others to see them. The film does slow down in the second half, and gets a tad repetitive, but keeps you with it.

And it brings to your attention the actors who never get their due in today's mainstream cinema. Kartika is fresh and perky. Sushant Singh is very good. But the real surprise in this package is Rajat Kapoor, who delivers a pitch-perfect performance as a man whose identity depends upon his designation, on what he can paint on his entrance plate below his name.

Jaideep Varma took many years to get this one out. His second should be sooner.

Saas Bahu Aur Sensex

CAST: Kirron Kher, Farooq Sheikh, Tanushree Dutta, Ankur Khanna, Lilette Dubey, Masumeh

DIRECTOR: Shona Urvashi

CAN women understand the complex world of finance, stocks and shares, and the Sensex? Or should they be confined to watching 'saas bahu' serials?

Shona Urvashi's second film has a whopper of an idea. And stalwarts fronting it. Kirron Kher is the divorced, desperately-in-need-of-money Binita Sen, who lands up at the door of Feroz Sethna, an eccentric out-of-work stock broker (Farooq Sheikh). He is rude and brusque. She is angry and annoyed. And then it turns into a profitable partnership, professional and personal.

The interplay between these two consummate actors could have taken Warner Brothers' first Indian production Saas Bahu Aur Sensex to an interesting place. But the director sends out confusing signals by gathering up a bunch of kitty-party aunties, converting them from couch potatoes to eager Economic Times-reading stock hounds, and then letting them slip, and lose money. What is she trying to say: can they or can't they? "Aaj sharad purnima hai, aaj toh Sensex zaroor upar jayega", intones Mrs Sen. Leaving the irascible Mr Sethna beaming, and, horrors, agreeing.

So is greed good? Mrs Sen, who's been picking up all the rising stocks unerringly, suddenly becomes all over-pious, and rants on about the evils of wanting to make money. Huh? In between, youngsters working on today's jobs crop up. Tanushree and Ankur are call centre execs, refining their Yank accents. Masumeh is a femme fatale, who wants 'moneh', not love.

In the end, it's so all-over-the place and indeterminate that you couldn't be bothered. What makes up for the rest is watching the inimitable Farooq in a full-fledged role, and Kirron as a non-stereotyped Bollywood mom, both after a long time.

— SHUBHRA GUPTA

shubhra.gupta@gmail.com

THREE MONKEYS

CAST: Yavuz Bingol, Hatice Aslan,

Rifat Sungar, Ercan Kesal

DIRECTOR: Nuri Bilge Ceylan

THERE are secrets within all families, and so the premise of Ceylan's award-winning Turkish film has everything going for it: a family that opts to stay together speaking no evil, hearing no evil and seeing no evil. Hence the title.

However, families hardly go about it in the detached manner that Ceylan films the story. Three Monkeys moves at a languorous pace, studded with meaningful glances and even-more-meaningful pauses, and it's hard to shake off the feeling that what we are seeing is more style than substance. It won him the best director award at Cannes 2008, and you can see why.

The story is essentially about four characters, Eyup (Bingol), wife Hacer (Aslan), son Ismail (Sungar) and Eyup's boss Servet (Kesal). Servet is a budding politician and one night just before the elections, he runs over someone. Afraid of the political fallout, he convinces his driver Eyup to take the rap for him, promising him a lump sum when he gets out.

Eyup is jailed for nine months. While his family doesn't lack of money, Hacer becomes increasingly lonely. On top of it she has on her hands a teenager son who has fallen into bad company. All this drives her to take a step that threatens to break the family.

While Aslan is convincing as guilt-ridden Hacer, unsure about what she should do next, the director fumbles badly with the denouement. The lack of dialogues may be a calculated move, but the film tries to make up with silences that scream threateningly loud about limited ideas on how to deal with the climax.

The men fare the poorest, swinging between extreme reactions and unclear passiveness. Hacer almost jumps off the terrace twice, and in one nice scene, after telling her to kill herself if she wants, Eyup pauses on his way out of the building, as if checking out the height.

However, we never understand why he does it — out of love, hatred or something in between. And that's the failing of Three Monkeys. We fathom all of it, and yet

almost none of it gets across.

— SHALINI LANGER

shalini.langer@expressindia.com

Heading: Quirk of fate: Champs tossed out - Indian Express
Content:
Cards 68 amid tough conditions to move a shot behind leader Bhullar

A sturdy umbrella figured big in survival essentials on the golf course on a drenched Friday. A look at Jyoti Randhawa's second round should have been made mandatory too.

By the time the morning squalls had turned into an incessant pour by the afternoon and players struggled with pars, Randhawa sneaked up with a copybook round of four-under, finding himself right in the thick of things for the DLF Masters weekend.

Gaganjeet Bhullar's painstaking par effort still has him holding onto the lead, though of just a lone shot over Randhawa. Thursday's second-placed Harmeet Kahlon and third-placed Himmat Singh Rai got stuck in the muddy mire, shooting four-over and five-over respectively to drop down. Shamim Khan's disciplined three-birdie, two-bogey effort has brought him into third place, three shots off Bhullar's five-under 139.

When the cloudy morning's play started, though, Bhullar looked to be in trouble even before warming up. He got the hedges on the left off his tee shot on the par-four tenth, his first hole, and somehow managed to take four shots in getting to the green, giving him a double bogey to start out.

Amends were literally round the bend, though, with a stunning tee shot on the par-three 11th landing four feet away from the pin for an easy birdie. He then missed short birdie putts on the 13th and 14th holes. But as the rain started, Bhullar squelched around roughs as he missed fairway after fairway, barely managing to keep his score in check.

"The ball kept getting muddy, making it hard to control. Also, my ball would hit the fairway and bounce out into the rough," Bhullar explained later. "I think it was unlucky."

The 20-year-old should probably be thanking his putter, though, as several nervy moments were warded off and the string of pars stayed unbroken. Then on the par-three eighth, Bhullar hit his eight-iron to 16 feet away and tucked it right in for the day's second birdie, finally erasing the one-over for the round from his scorecard.

Randhawa, though, had no troubles sticking to fairways, despite his later admission that the wet course was "playing twice as long."

Starting in the afternoon from the 10th, it was quiet at the start, with two straight bogeys on the 12th and the 13th making it seem like another ordinary day. The round, though, came alive with a 25-foot putt on the par-three 16th for his first birdie. He followed that up with another long birdie putt on the 17th to be even par at the turn.

The major upheavel, however, came on the back nine. Great control off the tee set up three small birdie putts on the fourth, sixth and seventh holes, before a 15-foot eagle attempt on the ninth stayed short of that thumping finish, but was good enough for the day's sixth birdie.

Playing in the same group, Gaurav Ghei also turned around Thursday's forgettable show with a one-under that puts him in tied 13th spot with a two-over 146.

Shiv Kapur's fortune revival will have to wait. A six-over 78 to follow the first round's 76 made sure he won't be back for the weekend rounds, though with the cut coming at a huge nine-over, his one-stroke miss would hurt even more.

Heading: Rashid grabs second straight amateur title - Indian Express
Content:
NCC (North East Region) skipper Dennisa Lalchhuawma looked inconsolable while informing his team mates about their exit from this year's Subroto Cup.

Being the defending champions and failing to make the quarter-finals wasn't the only reason behind the scenes — it also had to do with the fact that their fate was decided by a coin toss.

Despite their 4-1 thrashing of Goa on Friday, NCC (NER) lost out on the toss after striking a deadlock on goal difference (-1) with NCC (West Bengal & Sikkim). Friday's other result — the NCC (WB&S) team losing 2-5 to Orissa made things more painful for the Mizoram boys.

And if this wasn't enough, team supervisor Pankaj Kanwar was quick to add another point. "The worst part is we won 4-0 against them in the qualifying rounds. There should have been a re-match. But we had to abide by the rules," said Kanwar.

'Unfortunate'

Dennisa Lalchhuawma, however, denied describing it as merely 'unfortunate'.

"We have defeated them 4-0 in the qualifying rounds. But today, we could have scored more goals. We just missed too many chances," rued Lalchhuawma.

A four-goal victory was all they needed, but fell one short after coming close to scoring at least three more.

For the time being, NCC (WB & S) supervisor Rajesh Kumar looked pleased with the turn of events, and would draw inspiration from a bit of history — Army XI went on to lift the Durand Cup in 2005 after snatching a semi-final berth from Dempo Sports Club on draw of lots after the teams had been deadlocked on goal difference.

The result, however, will be remembered for making a first in the 48-year-old history of Subroto Cup.

Other results

U-14: St. Ignatius High School, Jharkhand beat MP Sports College, Dehradun, Uttarakhand 4-0, Green Wood Hr Sec School, Nagaland defeated BKSP, Bangladesh 2-1. Sukantanagar Vidyaniketan,West Bengal bt Namchi Sports Hostel, Sikkim 1-0, NCC (WB & S) lost to Town School, Orissa 5-2.

Heading: Coming Full Circle - Indian Express
Content:
IT was a professional dismissal of all possible challengers. Rashid Khan shot his second straight five-under 67 for a whopping eight-shot victory at the Golden Greens gof course on Friday, his second straight win on the LG Indian Amateur Tour.

The overnight leader by one shot, Rashid raced ahead of the pack with a four-under by the time he finished his front nine. After that, it was just a matter of keeping steady and he did exactly that. The chasing pack never really had a chance, left to fight over the second spot, a battle won by Rudresh Sharma with an even par round.

Promising star

But the day belonged to Rashid, who has quickly emerged as the most promising star on the amateur circuit. Reflecting on his show this week, Rashid said: "I am very happy considering that I have just started playing on the amateur tour. It gives me a lot of confidence."

With just one bogey through the last two rounds — it came on Friday on the par-four 17th — Rashid was sublime through the decisive part of the tournament.

Rashid was off to a sedate start this week but he said: "Even on the first day I was playing pretty well till a triple bogey on the eighth put messes up the round."
