Admitted at the Trauma Centre in AIIMS sustaining bullet wound in his right arm in yesterday's gunbattle with the alleged militants, Rana said, "I had a special relationship with Sharma-sir: he treated me like a member of his own family. His death is not just a personal loss, it is a great loss for Delhi Police.

"Indeed, a loss for the entire nation."

Rana underwent operation on Friday evening to extract the bullet that had entered his elbow. "The doctors have said they have fixed my damaged elbow and asked me to take complete rest for a week," Rana said. Feeling "dizzy" following excessive blood loss, Newsline did not want to stress him further.

Rana maintained that he was feeling fine — "just a little weak."

Meanwhile, as the police department was busy with Sharma's cremation, Rana's friends, colleagues and family members kept up a vigil at the hospital to check on his condition. "He is conscious now and feeling much better," Rana's sister, Saroj Devi, said. "My brother is a very brave policeman, and was posted at the Special Cell for his bravery."

The casualty medical officer at AIIMS's Trauma Centre, Dr M C Mishra, also said Rana is now stable: "The bullet had passed through his arm and the wound is still big. His arm has been fractured and he underwent operation last evening.

"He needs to be under medical supervision for the next four or five days at least."

Rana's wife Pinki and children Madhav, 4, and Varsha, 11, who live with his parents in UP's Bulandsheher reached Delhi last evening.

Rana joined Delhi Police in 1996 as a constable with the 4th Battalion and was posted at Kingsway Camp police station. In 2000, he was transferred to Gandhinagar in East District, where he stayed till 2003. He was subsequently posted at Mayur Vihar police station, till 2005, after which he cleared an examination to be a head constable.

Rana's next posting was with the Special Cell.

Heading: Cops get 14-day custody of arrested militants - Indian Express
Content:
Police Commissioner Y S Dadwal on Saturday ordered all Delhi Police inspectors and duty officers at police stations to carry their service weapon throughout duty hours, sources said.

Sources said Dadwal reiterated the decision, earlier issued some four months ago, at a meeting on Saturday morning. The order comes a day after Inspector Mohan Chand Sharma died leading the encounter at Jamia Nagar in South Delhi.

Dadwal made it clear that strict action would be taken against any officer found without the mandatory service pistol or revolver on him. The meeting, which lasted about 45 minutes, included all inspector-level officers apart from the brass of Delhi Police. Besides routine discussions on security arrangements in the Capital, it was "decided in the meeting that all inspectors, duty officer at all police stations, Reader of the Station House Officer will compulsorily keep a pistol or a revolver," a police source said.

The source added that "deeply affected" by Inspector Sharma's death, Dadwal issued the instruction to "his men" to be more alert and vigilant".

According to sources, the instruction was also an outcome of increasing ambush fire against police officers in the Capital. "Friday's incident was an example of a surprise attack by the militants," the source said. "This step has been taken to thwart such incidents in future."

Delhi Police spokesperson Rajan Bhagat said, "As per the situation, the Commissioner of Police asked his men to be vigilant, and carrying a weapon was one of the important points he made in the meeting."

Bhagat said Dadwal also told his officers that they should be fully prepared for any counter-terrorism operation from now on.

Heading: Parents worried back home, brigade from Azamgarh tense in city - Indian Express
Content:
Mohammed Saif and Zeeshan, the two suspected militants arrested after Friday's encounter in Jamia Nagar for their involvement in September 13 serial blasts, were remanded to 14 days police custody by a city court today.

During the hearing, the Special Cell, probing into the serial blasts, told the court of Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (ACMM) Kanwaljit Arora that preliminary investigations revealed that the two were involved in the blast at Gaffar Market in Karol Bagh. The Cell told the court that the duo's custodial interrogation was necessary to arrest co-conspirators.

ACP (Special Cell) Sanjeev Yadav also told the court that during their interrogation, the two had disclosed that 10 others, now absconding, were involved in Saturday's blasts.

ACMM Arora said, "Considering the abhorrent and fiendish acts that rattled Delhi last Saturday and investigating agency was also bereaved of an officer and to unearth the conspiracy, both the accused are remanded to 14-day police custody."

Saif, son of a local politician from Azamgarh in Uttar Pradesh, was arrested after Friday morning's encounter in South Delhi's Jamia Nagar. Zeeshan was taken into custody from a news channel's studio at Jhandewalan later in the evening.

Heading: Goodbye, braveheart - Indian Express
Content:
As jamia Nagar limped back to normalcy a day after the encounter, its populous 'migrant' population — 5,000-odd youths from Azamgarh, in eastern Uttar Pradesh — are anxious about their future in the national capital. With the alleged militants gunned down or arrested in yesterday's encounter all coming from Azamgarh, the youths here say their parents would much rather have them return home.

Official sources say there are 5,000 registered voters in Jamia Nagar belonging to Azamgarh. According to officials, at least 2,000 people without a voter's identity card — all primarily students — live on rent in the area.

Abu Zarr, an MA (Arabic) student at Jamia Millia Islamia, says: "As TV channels kept repeating that the 'terrorists' are from Azamgarh, they (parents back home) got scared and called me up. They are asking me to leave studies and go back.

"Even I am scared, but I can't just leave studies and go."

Others like him are equally confused. Shahzad Alam, a PhD student of Political Science at Jamia, says he has already received many calls from family asking him to go back. "I am scared here, because I also stay on rent," he says. "If I go back, the police will suspect that I have fled and the next thing I know, they are hot on my trail.

"If I stay, what guarantee do I have about my security here?"

And it's not just the students: Abdul Rababul, a businessman renting a place in Batla House for the past few years, says his family is calling up repeatedly. "They want me to return; they feel Delhi is not safe for me," Rababul says. "I tried to reason with them but my parents keep insisting that I go back. I don't know if the encounter was fake or not but over the past some years, a lot of people from Azamgarh have been targeted.

"I am also scared, to tell the truth, but I can't leave my business just like that."

Heading: Alms and the Man - Indian Express
Content:
Saturday, 3.30 pm. All roads leading to Nigam Bodh Ghat were lined with white Ambassador cars as traffic police officers scurried around, manning them.

For the first time in the history of Delhi Police, four former Police Commissioners — M B Kaushal, T R Kakkar, Ajai Raj Sharma and K K Paul — were present together to bid a final farewell to an inspector. Police officers of all ranks, many of whom had never even worked with the deceased, were present at Nigam Bodh Ghat.

And they were all bidding farewell to a hero: Inspector Mohan Chand Sharma, who died in the gunbattle with alleged militants in Jamia Nagar on Friday.

Not just police brass, even politicians across party lines came to pay final tributes. Union Home Minister Shivraj Patil, Minister of State for Home Sriprakash Jaiswal, senior BJP leader L K Advani, Lieutenant Governor Tejendra Khanna, Chief Minister Sheila Dikshit and scores of BJP and Congress politicians from the Capital were present.

Amid a sea of khaki, Inspector Sharma's body was brought on a flower-decked Delhi Police truck. The 12 ceremonial guards fired three rounds from their .303 rifles and the 'Last Post' was played in the background as cries of "Jai Bharat Mata" and "Jai M C Sharma" rent the air. Several other mourners who had also come to bid a final farewell to their loved ones forgot their personal grief and stood watching the grand procession.

Police Commissioner Y S Dadwal and Joint Commissioner Karnal Singh carried Sharma's body.

Sharma's close associate, Assistant Sub Inspector Prahlad Meena, who had worked with him for the past 12 years, broke down. Meena had been running around since morning at Sharma's Dwarka residence, making arrangements for the last rites. At the cremation, however, he could not hold back his tears any longer.

Also crying inconsolably was Sub-Inspector Dharmendar, the first police official to go to the flat housing the alleged militants posing as a salesman and who later carried Sharma to the hospital. In a daze almost the whole of Friday in bloodstained clothes, Dharmendar was quiet since Saturday morning. Assistant Sub-Inspector Anil Tyagi, who had also worked with Sharma, had been controlling crowd since morning. Weary and anxious, he shouted time and again, pleading with the crowd to give space for his senior's body.

Sharma's 14-year old son Divyanshu could not perform the last rites since he continues to be unwell — the boy is in hospital with dengue.

Heading: Fringe Players - Indian Express
Content:
An ex-army man turns crusader for the cause of young and physically challenged beggars on the streets of Gurgaon

Eight-year-old Sunny Kumar, son of a daily wage labourer, has only one functional limb. Missing a right arm at birth, Sunny was forced to beg on the streets for his survival. For him, studying in a school was a distant dream. But thanks to Apni Duniyan Apni Aashiyan (ADAA), the dream has come true.

The man who made it possible is 35-year-old Navin Gulia, who quit the Army 13 years ago following a spinal injury that left him wheelchair-bound. Now he is endeavouring to make Gurgaon roads beggar-free with his organisation ADAA, which works for orphans and the physically challenged who have taken to the streets. Conceptualised last year, the organisation aims to set up a shelter for them by the end of this year. At present there are nearly 1,200 children begging on the streets of Gurgaon, of which about 700 are forced beggars. ADAA is providing food, medicines and basic education to about 250 child-beggars.

Felicitated with the National Role Model Award for 2006 by the then President Abdul Kalam and with several other achievements to his credit, Gulia also made it to the Limca Book of World Records in 2005 for driving 55 hours at a stretch through seven of the highest mountain passes in the world to reach Marsimik La 18,634 feet. "Adventure is not about taking risks, it's about eliminating risk. A sportsman looks at difficulties as challenges," Gulia says.

The real battle, adds Gulia, is one that must be fought off the field, "against the corruption, indifference and lethargy that pervade the society". The society, he says, has turned a blind eye to underprivileged children. Instead of trying to bail them out of the situation, he says, people compound the beggar problem by giving coins to street children. Gulia has been striving to raise awareness and discourage people from donating small change. ADAA wants to bring to the notice of the administration the problem of the children on the streets.

He attributes the governmental apathy to votebank politics. "These children cannot vote. They don't even have a voice," he says. Although voluntary contributions are coming in, only a fraction of them actually reach him because of the corruption in the system. Yet, Gulia is undaunted and plans to launch initiatives to generate funds for the proposed shelter. He is planning a 40-day cross-country road expedition called 'One India Campaign' to generate funds. Gulia will travel along the periphery of India, covering a distance equal to half the length of the equator, that is, over 20,000 km.

Gulia plans to write a book about the challenges he had to face. He feels his achievements have no meaning if he does not do anything for the society. "Your ability never restricts you, your thoughts do. If you think you can, you can," he says, as he works for a day when there won't be a single child asking for alms on the streets of Delhi.

For more information go to www. adaa.in or call 9810245996

Heading: A school that rocks - Indian Express
Content:
Since 1997, Pandies Theatre has been working with people who live on the margins of society

Every time we think we've seen the worst of the world, a new bottomless pit opens up and we are confronted by another, more terrible hell," says Sanjay Kumar, whose group, Pandies Theatre, since 1997, has been working with people who live on the margins of society—in slums, on railway platforms, in riot-scarred ghettos.

"We are Pandies," says Kumar referring to the word used by British commanders who could not pronounce Pandey, a reference to Mangal Pandey. "Pandie is an expletive pronounced with an ejection of spit at the end. Pandie, a term even more hated, more despised than the English traitor. We are Pandies of modern India, in a constant subversive relation with all that our mainstream culture and its values represent," he adds.

Pandies' roots go back to 1987 when a handful of teachers and students of Delhi University attempted to do meaningful theatre. "Early on, we decided that patriarchal modes have failed and if we want to inhabit a better world it, has to be more woman-oriented." They called themselves a feminist theatre group and one of their constant efforts involves homosexual women in deprived areas. "Amazingly, the more deprived people are, the more keen they are on theatre," he says.

In November 2005, the group—comprising about 75 members, mostly university students and teachers—was invited to a school in Nithari. "Children are natural actors with an inherent need for self-expression," he says. During the once-a-week classes with the Nithari youngsters, the group often encountered rumours of missing children. "But nothing had prepared us for what would happen next," he recalls. Even as the police unearthed the horrors of Nithari in Noida where skulls and bones of missing children were discovered in December 2006, Kumar noticed that the children had turned horribly silent. "Some of them had narrowly escaped being killed, others had siblings who had been murdered," he says. With little prodding from the theatre group, the children groups independently created three skits, all of which showed tiny bodies being chopped. "It is a comment on our times that two of the skits ended with the accused bribing the police and escaping," says Kumar.

Work in Nithari continues, but three months ago Pandies arrived at a village in Badarpur Khadar. "We found four villages, flanked by UP on three sides and with the Yamuna on the fourth. Caught between Delhi and UP, the villages have no electricity or proper healthcare facilities and only a handful of the children have been to school. Yet, they have a strong urge to study," he says. Pandies members spend more than an hour teaching the children English, Hindi, mathematics and art. "And then, theatre takes over and it is our turn to learn from what the children have to tell us," says Kumar.

Children are always a revelation, he says. For instance, at a workshop with children who live in the Delhi railway stations, a nine-year-old boy whispered that he loved Rajdhani and Shatabdi trains. "I wondered why? Then, to my horror, I found out that the boys would get paid hefty sums to be sexually exploited in the bathrooms. Also, because the dustbins of these trains contain good food."

Pandies' new production, he says, will be on "issues that should be election issues but never are" and will be held at the Shri Ram Centre. But for these rebels, the stage will remain the poorest localities of the Delhi and its surroundings. "Because in the milieu of the disempowered one has to act. To act is to perform; to act is also to do and to change."

Heading: Photo Op - Indian Express
Content:
After the success of Rock On, the Noida School of Rock climbs up the popularity charts

When Anmol Rai came back to the city after completing his studies from the Trinity College of Music in London a few years ago, he realised there were no schools in and around Delhi for rock music. "I came across so many people who were talented and just needed a platform to showcase it. I also realised that they needed to be trained in the same way as musicians are abroad," he says. So, he decided to start the Noida School of Rock.

The school has 300-odd students who are learning an instrument—keyboard, guitar, drums, violin—or are receiving vocal training. "The teachers are all professionally trained and we use the best equipment to teach our students," says 28-year-old Rai, who also performs with iWitness and Perfect Strangers, both Delhi-based bands. Rai, who is a visiting faculty at Miranda House, also teaches music in DPS Noida.

NSR conducts an annual concert in which more than 30 student bands take part. They also perform in pubs and clubs during Christmas and New Year's Eve. All students get a chance to perform on stage through these concerts. "Our aim is to make sure that each and every student in the school gets a chance to showcase their talent in front of a crowd. This gives them the confidence and makes them feel like a rock star," says Rai. The students get to form their own bands and cover songs that range from country singers like John Denver to metal-heads such as Pantera and Megadeath.

To get admissions in the school is easy. Rai takes an informal interview to gauge a applicant's talent. Also, there is no age limit—the youngest student is five-year-old Malvika Dang, a hardcore metal fan and a budding guitarist, and the oldest is 60-year-old Amit Verma who learns the keyboards. "Music knows no boundaries, no religion and no age. We didn't want to intimidate people by setting an age limit or a tough entrance exam and interview," he says.

The tough bit begins after the admissions. Every student has to appear for an end-term exam that is conducted under the supervision of visiting lecturers from Trinity College of Music and Rock School, London. Another achievement for the school is that the highest number of toppers in these exams that are held in Malaysia, Hong Kong, Thailand, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Singapore, the UAE and India, are from the Noida school.

Even though the school has been around for close to three years, Rai agrees that its popularity has gone up after the release of Farhan Akhtar's Rock On. "As a musician, I found the movie extremely inspiring and motivating," he says.

Heading: Autopsy suggests Sharma died of ‘excessive bleeding’ - Indian Express
Content:
From next month, one of the city's oldest studios, the Delhi Photo Company, will start functioning as a gallery for photo exhibitions

Time was when Connaught Place was dotted with well known photo studios. People would come all the way from Kalkaji in south Delhi to get a 'good' photo taken at Rangoon or Shimla photo studio and get the roll they shot on during their weekend trip to Agra processed at Mahatta's. Today, with digital cameras around, getting a family photo taken by a professional photographer is a thing of the past. "So what was once Rangoon studio is now Pizza Hut and Shimla studio has turned into Barista," smiles photographer Ajay Shanker of the Delhi Photo Company, one of the oldest studios in the city.

When an automobile major approached Delhi Photo Company to buy the outlet for a car showroom, the Shankers refused to part with their shop. The offer was tempting, but they had a different plan—that of converting 2,000 square feet of their shop into a gallery exclusively for photo exhibitions. The plan also included a café with kitchen, a backyard-turned-into a garden for evening get-togethers, and a place where photographers —both veterans and amateurs— could meet and exchange ideas.

Standing behind the counter in the shop, Ajay Shanker hardly has the airs of a Bollywood photographer. Perhaps those who come here to buy a camera film are not even aware that from Tango Charlie to Matrubhoomi to Dil Maange More to Thanks Maa (a film that was sent as an entry to the Cannes film festival this year), Shanker has shot the publicity material for several Hindi films in the last six years.

During the last two years he has been painstakingly restoring the studio and turning it into a gallery. The result is that from old Gothic pillars to wooden staircases have been restored and antique cameras, photographs of erstwhile maharajas and nawabs can be spotted in the gallery along with magazines and brochures on photography. As a part of the experiment, Shanker has also organised an exhibition by students of the College of Art. However, the gallery will formally open in October.

"Photography is seen more as a business than an art form these days. There are no galleries that exclusively display photographs and give a platform to both professionals and students of photography. I want this gallery to be sans a commercial tag and definitely not a meeting place for Page 3 celebrities," says Shanker, adding that at least once a month he wants to screen documentaries and hold book-reading sessions at the gallery.

Opening the city's first full-fledged photography gallery is certainly an ambitious project and Shanker has spent nearly

Rs 15 lakh in making his dream come true.

But for Shanker, no obstacle is big enough to come between him and his dream. His father, Vijay Shanker, was the first Indian photographer to be trained in Germany and their company was also the first official photographer of the President of India. With such family history to fall back upon, Shanker is confident his gallery has a bright future.

Heading: HC looks at interim compensation for Blueline victims’ families - Indian Express
Content:
Doctors at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), who performed the autopsy on encounter specialist Mohan Chand Sharma, did not find any bullet in his body and said he died due to "excessive internal bleeding".

"In these kinds of cases, an X-Ray is done before conducting the postmortem for thoroughly screening the body. The X-Ray did not show any bullets inside his body. No bullets were found even in the autopsy. The bullet could have penetrated and then exited his body," a senior AIIMS doctor said.

This, experts say, usually happens during close quarter shootings and when a high-velocity firearm is used. "The wound suggests it was a near shot from a rifled firearm. These have greater accuracy and stability," another doctor said.

Special Cell inspector and top encounter cop Mohan Chand Sharma was killed in Friday's encounter in Jamia Nagar, which lasted for over an hour. Two men, who the police claim were behind the serial blasts in Delhi, Ahmedabad and Hyderabad, were also killed.

The doctors said the wounds on Sharma's body suggest he was hit by two bullets — one in the stomach and the other on his arm. "The bullet usually exits if it enters soft tissue, as in this case where it hit the stomach and arm. If the bullet had hit a bone, it would have shattered," the doctor added. "The cause of death is shock due to loss of excessive blood," the doctor said.

Forensic experts at AIIMS, however, have not yet handed over the postmortem report to the police and have asked for the report of the doctor at Holy Family who treated the inspector before he succumbed to his injuries. "While it is quite difficult to take out bullets during surgery, to make sure before we present our conclusions, we have asked for the surgical intervention report from the police," a doctor said.

Meanwhile, the bodies of the two terror suspects killed in the encounter are lying at the AIIMS mortuary. The police are looking for claimants but experts say if no one comes forward to claim the bodies, a postmortem can be carried out in such cases after 72 hours.

Heading: Planned in detail, bombs came from Karnataka - Indian Express
Content:
Blueline owners now have one more reason to caution their drivers against reckless driving. In a step which might prove to be the most "effective deterrent" against the rising accident graph of Bluelines in the Capital, the Delhi High Court on Saturday indicated towards a decision to award "immediate" interim compensation to victims' families to help tide over the tragedy.

A Bench comprising Chief Justice A P Shah and Justice S Muralidhar said Blueline owners will have to cough up Rs 1 lakh as interim compensation to victims' families in case of fatal accidents and Rs 50,000 to those with grievous injuries or permanent disability as the result of the mishap. The court will pass written orders in the case on September 24.

The court has also asked the Delhi Transport Corporation to file a response on whether the public carrier would be amenable to having a similar scheme for accident victims as well.

The Bench views the interim scheme as a humanitarian move to provide sustenance in the form of financial assistance for Blueline victims and their families during the time the bus owner is tried in a court of law.

The case was heard after the High Court, in July 2007, took suo motu cognizance of the increasing number of fatalities involving Blueline buses. Explaining the scheme, the Bench said the Blueline bus would immediately be impounded after such an accident and released by the Metropolitan Magistrate only after the owner pays interim compensation.

"The Magistrate himself will take the deposit from the Blueline owner at the time of the release," amicus curiae A J Bambhani said, "The compensation amount, whether in the case of death or grievous injuries, will be handed over to the victims or his family by the Magistrate himself."

To receive the amount, the victim or his/her family will give a written undertaking in the court to file a motor accidents claim case in the Special Tribunal for a final decree on the compensation amount.

"The amount given by the Magistrate is only for immediate help to the victims— the final compensation will be given through the insurance claim on the vehicle as ordered by the Tribunal," said Bhambhani.

The amount provided as interim compensation will later be adjusted with the final amount of compensation as ordered by the Special Tribunal.

"The interim compensation given by the bus owner will be reimbursed to him by the insurance company after the Tribunal passes its final orders," the amicus added.

The court foresees a major role etched out for the Delhi Police in accident cases where the victims are from a financially weak background. "The police will immediately notify the Delhi Legal Services.

Authority (DLSA) which will provide free legal aid to victims seeking interim compensation from the Magistrate court," said the amicus curiae.

Heading: Sharma knew exactly what he was doing: Cell chief - Indian Express
Content:
Last Saturday's bombings were planned by Atif and Tauqeer long ago. Atif and 13 of his accomplices first brought 10 bombs three days before Ramzan started from one Shahrukh in Karnataka. The police said Shahrukh has supplied bombs to Atif for the Ahmedabad blasts, the UP court blasts, Jaipur blasts and now Delhi; and is now an important man to catch. "Shahrukh even went with a module of 11 persons to Ahmedabad, where they manufactured bombs. The Karnataka police has been alerted about him," a source said.

The Special Cell has learnt from Zeeshan and Saif's interrogation that for the Delhi blasts, Atif and Tauqeer first carried out a recce of the markets and crowded places where the bombs where to be planted two days before the blasts. Tauqeer reportedly left for Mumbai a day before the blasts. Also a day before, Atif, Saif and Khalid reportedly brought the bombs from Karnataka. They travelled in trains using fake identity documents.

They then attached analogue watches to the bombs as timers on Saturday morning in L-18 in Batla House. Each bomb was set to go off after 6 pm, with a gap of 5 to 10 minutes between each blast. They all left their mobile phones in the flat.

In the evening, they left L-18 in autorickshaws. Shakil went to Ghaffar Market and left the bomb in the auto itself. Zeeshan (whose face also matches with one of the sketches made by the Delhi Police and has been arrested) and Sajid (who was killed in Friday's encounter) went to Barakhamba and placed a bomb in an NDMC garbage bin. Saif (who is in Special Cell custody) and Khalid kept two in garbage bins outside Regal Cinema in Connaught Place. Atif (IM leader) himself and Junaid went to the Greater Kailash market and kept two bombs in dustbins there. Sajid went to the Central Park on his own and planted two bombs there in dustbins. Shehzad Bhai, alias Mallick, had gone to India Gate and he kept a bomb there in a bin in the Children's Park. They all had placed the bombs around 6 pm.

After planting the bombs, they returned in autorickshaws to the flat and turned on the TV. They did not switch on their cell phones for the next few hours. They had all returned to the flat by 7.45 pm.

Two out of the three unexploded bombs did not explode because they malfunctioned after they were thrown in bins from a distance.

They, Delhi Police say, dumped the tenth bomb in a drain in Batla House and the cops are looking for it.

The police said they were staying in two hideouts; the other hideout has yet to be traced. Officers suspect that 10 absconding terrorists might be holed up there and that the police could also find other material and explosives from this hideout.

Heading: ‘Shaken, shocked’, next door youths back home - Indian Express
Content:
Upset over the death of his Special Cell's best man, Joint Commissioner of Police Karnal Singh could not check his emotions when a mediaperson asked him on Saturday why Inspector Mohan Chand Sharma was not wearing a bulletproof jacket during the encounter. Furious, Singh shot back that Sharma was absolutely meticulous with his plan, and that he was "not a novice".

"He was an expert in his field and knew what to do in such circumstances," Singh said. "He would not go wearing a bulletproof jacket there as he knew that those hiding (in the building) might get alerted."

Singh said Sharma had conducted encounters in Kashmir also and knew to the last details each of his operations and what he was getting into. Instead of pointing fingers, Singh said, "we should appreciate the courage he showed — he has showed the way to all of us to fight for our country. We must admit that we will miss him in future."

Initially, before informing the media about the police's breakthroughs in September 13 serial blasts case, Singh expressed sorrow at losing Delhi Police's 'best man': "I worked with Mohan Chand for over four years and I had never seen him tired. His analytical (work) and fieldwork was unparalleled.

"We will always miss him."

As far as Friday's encounter is concerned, Singh said the inspector had the input but not specifically of the right address — there was reportedly some confusion about the house in which the alleged militants were holed up.

Joint Commissioner of Police, Special Cell, Karnal Singh, cleared some questions put forth by Newsline.

Ques: How many bullets hit Mohan Chand Sharma yesterday when he was heading an operation?

Three bullets hit him during operation when was fighting with the terrorists. He knew that he was going for an operation and it was not for the first time he was going to catch a terrorist. He knew that going without bulletproof jackets can alert the terrorists. He decided and planned his visit. We have lost a man who was full of energy, had good analytical abilities and whose field working was unparalleled. He worked hard and got the exact location of the terrorists.

Ques: What help did you get through interception and by checking Call Detail Reports of various cell numbers?

We did our technical analysis very well and it worked well for the case. A lot of numbers were verified. We cannot disclose the details as investigations are going on and terrorists can take advantage of it.

Ques: Have you found any fingerprint reports?

Fingerprint experts are working on those aspects. (However, Alok Kumar (DCP, Special Cell) earlier in the day had told Newsline, "We have not found any fingerprints from bomb sites.")

Ques: How are you tracking the other members who are absconding?

We are working on it. At this moment nothing can be disclosed because a lot of people are at large. —ENS

Heading: Jamia Nagar wakes up, still irate - Indian Express
Content:
The six teenagers, who were picked up by Special Cell officers on Friday after the encounter with three alleged terrorists in Batla House area, were released in the early hours of Saturday. The teenagers reside in flat number 107, opposite the one where the alleged terrorists were living (108).

Relatives of the boys said that "they were too shocked to speak".

While police claimed that it was protective detention prior to the encounter, relatives said the boys were picked up after the operation.

The six teenagers — all cousin brothers — have been identified as: Shahbaz Hussain (a student of Class XII), Rooni (Class X), Amir Khan (Class XI), Abu Jaleel (Class X), Karamat Khan (MBA student) and Sohail Anwar — who had undertaken special studies in the Quran at Saharanpur. Relatives said Anwar had come to Delhi to lead special Ramzan prayers (Taraveeh).

Police sources had earlier said the boys were picked up following information that a 13-year-old boy was involved in the gang and played a vital part in making the bombs used in September 13 blasts. Police wanted to know whether they knew the boy.

"They were not harassed by police or ill-treated. The police allowed them to offer namaaz and even provided them food for breaking their fasts in the evening. But they are mere children and are terrified," their uncle, Tariq Masood said.

Their cousin and flatmate Shakeel Ahmad, an MBA student, said that he had left for classes at 8.30 am on Friday, or else he too would have been picked up. He said "The police should have had the courtesy to at least inform relatives before taking the children away."

The cousins' immediate families reside in Gaya, Bihar, and they had come here for studies. Their uncle, one Saad Ahmad, a software professional settled in New Zealand, pays rent for their flat.

Heading: IIT techies show the way: 3-D simulation to clear glitches in infrastructure projects - Indian Express
Content:
As life returns to normalcy, locals shoot back: Why didn't cops take us into confidence?

Batla House, ground zero of Friday morning's encounter, is still seething a day on. Seething at the police for keeping residents in the dark before zeroing in on the alleged militants.

The residents say Inspector Mohan Chand Sharma's life could have been saved had the police got in touch with the locals before the encounter.

"We have met central ministers, even Home Minister Shivraj Patil, and told them about the issues we face," Irfanullah Khan, convenor of Jamia Nagar Coordination Committee and a Samata Party member, told Newsline on Saturday. "Had the police told us that they suspect militants are holed up here we could have been of big help to them."

Khan, based in Batla House area of Jamia Nagar in South Delhi for the last "at least 20 years", has his house just about 100 metres from L-18, the building where the police shot two alleged militants and arrested another. There were reports that two of the suspects had fled in the shootout, and one of them, identified as Zeeshan, was nabbed from Jhandewalan last night.

Abdur Rehman Abid, secretary of the coordination committee, said the police should have taken the elders of the area into confidence because "people listen to the elders; they listen to members of the coordination committee."

Meanwhile, as life slowly crawled back to normalcy and shops opened shutters this morning, most residents avoided journalists. A day on, the mood was that of suspicion and mistrust. Shadab Khan, 20, an MBA student of Jamia Millia Islamia, said, "We never get to know the real picture. They (police and authorities) did not even show us faces of the alleged militants shot yesterday."

Area coordination committee member Khan said the police should have kept them in the know because "people get sensitive at a time like this — the holy month of Ramzan".

The area had witnessed riots and tension in the month of Ramzan last year: a police chowki was burnt down after a policeman allegedly insulted a religious man and the Quran. A police station was set up in the area subsequently.

The situation was tense even

after Friday's encounter but Khan and some professors from Jamia had helped calm down the protestors who had gathered outside L-18, barely a few metres from Khaliullah Mosque.

Fayyaz Ahmed Khan, a lecturer in Engineering at Jamia, was near the spot yesterday. On Friday he had told Newsline, "The failure of the system is apparent but we need to stick to the judgment of our brave policemen."

A day on, as the humdrum of daily grind returns, several locals said they would like to share that faith in the system, and would like the system to take them into confidence.

Heading: Tourists check out after blasts, budget hotels in ‘sensitive’ areas bear the brunt - Indian Express
Content:
When reams of paper and millions of data figures proved inadequate in explaining the idea of driving along the central verge to an average bus driver used to zigzagging through the Capital's roads, the authorities in charge decided to get visual simulation for the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) corridor to train drivers on manoeuvring a bus towards the central verge without causing damage to other vehicles. For this was required not any average 3-D animation model, but a simulation of the 6.8 km-long corridor between Ambedkar Nagar and Moolchand, which meant creating an environment where a bus driver feels like sitting in a bus and manning an object similar to the steering wheel of a bus through the virtual BRT corridor.

In came Shantanu Sharma (27) and Rajiv Dinesh (25), whose company Medulla Soft happens to be the only firm in the country which works on creating 3-D visual simulation for infrastructure projects in the country.

"We collected data on movement of traffic, number of vehicles, cycles and pedestrians using the corridor at different times of the day and collated data of our own for about 15 days. We then created a simulation of the corridor with features in real-time," says Sharma.

"The drivers get to drive through the virtual corridor in an environment which is similar to the 'real' corridor at a particular time," adds Dinesh who co-founded the firm with Sharma and mentor Anil Virmani, an IIT 1966 batch passout , three years ago.

While the firm is yet to find its footing in Delhi, the duo are working on pilot projects for a multi-level parking lot to be constructed by DMRC and traffic plans for the New Delhi Railway Station The firm has also made an impact abroad, already bagging projects in Hiroshima, LA and Paris.

"In Hiroshima we are working on creating a simulation for a flyover which has an accident-prone patch. The authorities are trying to pin-point the problem, which could lie in the alignment or the traffic movement. The simulation will help them in recognising the problem," says Sharma, agreeing that India is yet to wake up to the benefits of creating simulations while designing infrastructure projects.

"A simulation provides a feel of the situation in real-time, which helps figure out mistakes and improvise while implementing a project design," says Dinesh, who gave up a job with an MNC for a venture of his own after college.

"We chanced upon the idea three years ago during a technology fair, when we were trying to start a real estate portal. Simulation is big business abroad and we never knew about it," says Sharma, who had earlier dabbled with the idea of starting a BPO of his own. The new idea, though, hit the right chord and both Sharma and Dinesh visited Japan for an intensive training schedule.

"Our simulations have helped designers to clear glitches in projects like the BRT corridor and the Taj Expressway. It is surprising that we are yet to wake up to the concept. Infrastructure development is growing in India and we need to realise that there is more to it than just drawing designs and laying bricks," Sharma says.

Heading: MCD comes under fire over dengue situation - Indian Express
Content:
The first business adversely affected by the serial bomb blasts in the Capital has been that of budget hotels located at tourist spots and markets in the city. With tourists "scared" in the aftermath of the blasts, hotel-owners say they prefer to stay away from hotels which are located near "vulnerable sites".

Hotels in the Karol Bagh market have suffered the biggest losses after the Saturday blasts. Many of the hotels are situated close to Gaffar Market and many tourists staying in these hotels had witnessed the blasts and its aftermath. The market is divided into seven blocks and each block has two gates and a separate president. Darshan Lal, president of the Ajmal Khan Road Shopkeepers' Association, said, "Police constables with metal detectors have been appointed at every entry and exit points of the main market."

Raj Bhasin, manager of Mehar Castle Hotels, said, "There were 40 per cent reservations in my hotel, all of which have been cancelled after the bomb blasts."

Some hotel managers said they have taken two to three rounds of the market personally to check the security arrangements.

Paharganj Market, — also known as "Hotel Ganj"— is another hot spot for hotels. Hotel businesses in this area have also witnessed huge setbacks after the blasts. The scenario is no different although the area has witnessed no terror attack of late. Shopkeepers and hotel owners are on the alert and have already started taking "precautions" to avoid any untoward incident in "their area". CCTV cameras have been put up in hotels through personal initiative and the identification and luggage of every visitor are being checked.

President of Hotel Association Arun Gupta said, "The new DCP of the Central District has already assured us about getting a proper security system into place. We have asked for more security guards and metal detectors."

A bomb squad team had come to the market after the recent blasts and conducted checks in the whole market. General Secretary R S Arora of the Hotel Welfare Association of Paharganj said "We are keeping a watch over possible terrorist activity and trying to ensure that nobody checks into any hotel using forged identification documents."

Heading: ‘Current strain has moderate viral load‘ - Indian Express
Content:
With dengue cases on the rise, alarm bells are ringing for the MCD even outside hospital wards: striking employees and expired drug stocks are making the sting harder.

Some 2,500 mosquito breeding checkers are on strike since September 17 and 80,000 kg medicines have gone unused.

The MCD is responsible for ensuring breeding checks across the city and undertaking preventive and curative measures but an unrestrained rise in the number of dengue cases this year has the Congress Opposition in the MCD up in arms.

The breeding checkers, employed on a contract basis by the civic body, are demanding that their jobs be regularised. Their strike and relay fast at Town Hall has sparked off a controversy over their removal and new appointments: the civic body is about to engage another 420 workers. "Of the 3,200 checkers, only about 750 are reporting for work. We had recently advertised for 420 vacant posts, for which we have received 6,000 applications," MCD Public Health Committee chairman V K Monga said.

"If the strike is not resolved in two to three days, we may even think of hiring more new people, effectively ending the contracts of the striking workers," he said.

But Farhad Suri, former mayor and municipal councillor from Nizamuddin, said the checkers were striking work rightfully, as they are not only underpaid but also not properly equipped with dippers or even stationery to note cases of breeding. "The checkers, who do not get their pay regularly, are expected to buy stationery out of their own pocket. The workers are also not issued ID cards and with all the resentment they face from house-owners, they should be protected by the corporation," Suri said.

Amid the standoff, dengue cases are increasing rapidly in the city. Delhi has reported over 300 cases and two deaths so far this year and officials said cases are not expected to decline, at least till September-end.

MCD officials, however, maintain statistics show that, as compared to previous years, the situation is not so bad. In 2007, the number of dengue cases reported was 548 and in 2006 and 2005 it was 3,366 and 1,023, officials said. In 2006, there were around 38 dengue-related deaths and in 2005 there were nine. Though the figure dipped to one last year, this year two deaths have already been reported.

The civic body also claims it has conducted breed checks in as many as 1.38 crore houses till September 6 and found 70, 336 houses with larvae breeding in them. This is in contrast to 2.73 crore checks carried out throughout last year, with 95,898 detections of breeding, a smaller number when compared to this year's figures.

But the Opposition would hear of none of this and has cried foul over the expiry of medicines and their misuse.

"The Delhi government had sanctioned Rs 22 crore for initiating measures to combat dengue but the MCD has wasted a major portion of the amount on buying medicines. To add to that, a bulk of these medicines has expired," Suri said.

The civic body, however, refuted these allegations and maintained that medicines for dengue have not expired and are being used. It also said it has been doing its bit and has completed the sprinkling of disinfectants in 10,07,823 houses so far.

"Fogging is not a good option, as the mosquitoes have begun developing immunity to it. Issuing challans is also not an option. Instead of using punitive measures, we must join hands with the people and create awareness. Nobody would want mosquitoes breeding in their homes and people will cooperate if we step up our awareness programme," Monga said.

Heading: 57 candles - Indian Express
Content:
The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) has decided to store 4,000 OVI traps, procured from the Defence Research and Development Establishment (DRDE) in Gwalior, for next year. These traps contain a chemical that can be used to contain Aedes Aegypti mosquito breeding.

"The traps came in too late this season, which is why we are keeping them for next year. In any case, they are more useful in surveillance and not control," Dr V K Monga, chairman of the MCD's health committee, said.

The rationale is to start early next year. Experts said the situation could have been much worse if a particular type of the dengue virus was prevalent this year.

With breeding inspectors on strike, record rainfall and uncontrolled mosquito breeding, a moderate viral load of the prevalent Type 1 strain in mosquitoes is the only silver lining for the MCD.

During the 2006 outbreak, it was the Type 2 and 3 strains that were prevalent in the Capital.

The MCD had approached the DRDE last month to assess the viral load through tests on samples of mosquitoes taken from Delhi. "We had taken a few mosquitoes from different areas in the Capital to Gwalior. It is important to know the viral load because, sometimes, the mosquito population is high but the viral load is low and sometimes even a few mosquitoes with a high viral load can cause a dengue outbreak. We wanted to be sure," Monga said.

We now have an accurate idea of the breeding index in different areas of the city. Reports have shown the mosquitoes have a moderate viral load," he added.

The MCD had asked for the OVI traps, with the intention of controlling mosquito breeding in areas with high-density breeding. The traps work on a simple principle. They contain a chemical that lures mosquitoes and creates a false sense of security in the female mosquito, inducing it to lay eggs in the trap. The trap uses an "attracticide", a mixture of biological chemicals that attracts female mosquitoes to the breeding site. The Insect Growth Regulator (IGR) then prevents these eggs from hatching.

The method is effective because the regulator not only prevents hatching but even if some eggs do hatch, the larvae cannot attain adulthood and therefore cannot spread disease.

Heading: Green Flea - Indian Express
Content:
The panel discussion for Screen's The Big Picture (our third edition this year) was attended by eminent personalities from the Hindi film industry who exchanged their views on various issues related to cinema. An elite panel of eight film industry professionals discussed the topic 'New, Improved Bollywood: Are we ready to take on the world?'. The panel included prominent names like writer-lyricist Javed Akhtar, actor-director Anupam Kher, actor Farooque Sheikh, writer-lyricist Prasoon Joshi, director-turned-actor Farhan Akhtar, actor Shiney Ahuja, Saurabh Varma, Chief Marketing Officer, Reliance Big Picture and Pankaj Khandpur, Creative Director, Visual Computing Labs, Tata Elxsi. They discussed film industry trends and achievements which excited an audience that comprised a combination of both film and media personnel.

After a stimulating experience for the grey-cells, it was time to hit nightclub Enigma at the JW Marriott for a grand celebration. Amitabh Bachchan cut the anniversary cake and what followed was a pulsating evening that celebrated the success of one of the film industry's most respected publications.

Several Bollywood celebrities attended Screen's 57th birthday bash and the party went on till the early hours. Film legends, popular TV artistes, dashing newcomers and popular filmmakers were all part of the celebration. The guest-list included Shatrughan Sinha with Poonam Sinha, Manmohan Shetty, Govind Nihalani, David Dhawan, Poonam Dhillon, Anu Malik, Sanjay Gadhvi, Sanjay Gupta and Madhur Bhandarkar, Kailash and Arti Surendranath, Sachin Pilgoankar, Renuka Shahane and Ashutosh Rana, Shankar Mahadevan, Pritam, Aadesh Srivastava, Sajid Khan, Lilette and Ravi Dubey and young guns like Arjun Rampal, Sonu Nigam, Himmesh Reshammiya, Luke Kenny, Purab Kohli, Nishikant Kamat, Sikandar Kher, Meera, Ronit Roy, Manasi and Rohit Roy, Sonal Chauhan, Mughda Godse, Vidya Malavade and many others.

A successful and engaging discussion on the happy developments in the film industry followed by a merry evening of glamour and glitz—it was a perfect way to bring in Screen's 57th year in business.

Heading: Dance Trance - Indian Express
Content:
Mango Nation, an NGO working for the environment, flagged off the first of their flea market at the Lodi Garden restaurant that saw a mix of designer labels and upcoming brands sharing space. With 'Goa' as the theme, the open market sought to bring to Delhi the popular Anjuna flea market of Goa with its thatched-roofed kiosks that resembled tiny beach-side shacks. Adding to the Goan appeal was a live Goan band that belted out popular reggae and pop numbers.

The market was a delight for accessory lovers with handbags in bright yellows, hot pink and turquoise on offer by Mint and innovatively designed shoes by Swati Modo. JJ Valaya Magic Foundation's kiosk invited a lot of attention with its quirky pet-toys and colourful T-shirts. Jewellery, candles and collector's items such as gold and silver plated handpicked flowers were on display. "The response has been amazing and in the past hour, we have already sold five bags," said Sheena Matharu, designer, Mint.

Planned as a monthly event, the flea market will be hosted with a special theme, working around music, art and food promotions. Vendors have to pay between Rs 6000-10,000 for a stall space. "The money collected from the stall prices will help in expanding our NGO' s initiative of planting more trees in the city," says Monica Batra of Mango Nation. Way to go.

Heading: American Diaries - Indian Express
Content:
When German dancer Antje Pfundtner began composing a piece based on her own life in 2003, she had no idea it would take her to places as far away as Lyon, Vienna, Riga, Helsinki, Rio de Janeiro, Bogota, Beijing, Brussels and even Pakistan.

Last week, Pfundtner stopped by Delhi and the response was the same as everywhere else — the audience watched her contort her limbs into impossible angles and went home convinced this 32-year-old doesn't have a single bone in her body. "The great thing about contemporary dance is that there is no restriction of movement," says Pfundtner.

It's the same spirit of independence that her piece Eigensinn salutes. Eigensinn merges rapid dance steps with breathless monologues of Pfundtner's journey from a newborn who doctors said would never walk. "They said I would have to live in a wheelchair," says the dancer before dragging her body, one stiff leg at a time, on to a chair. But, Pfundtner not only taught herself to move but also to dance. Once again, the rebel won.

When she teaches students at a dance workshop organised by Gati, Pfundtner is careful about freedom of expression and she says she encourages students to tap their own individuality. "I bring to them only the tools, the creativity is always their own," smiles Pfundtner. Look out for some new steps.

Heading: Cash at judge’s door: What’s the motive? CBI officials scratch their heads - Indian Express
Content:
American documentary photographer Matt Brandon, 50, says he'd had enough of typical images of foreigners being ferried around on rickshaws through Old Delhi. "I wanted to get into the crowded streets of Old Delhi and shoot the area's many architectural marvels, its people and culture," says Brandon, (pictured in the red T-shirt) who has been holding photography workshops in Old Delhi for foreign travelers, called "Lumen Dei" since 2007. Lumen Dei, which literally translates from Latin into "Light of God", is a two-week workshop that tries to, as Brandon puts it, "follow in the footsteps of the Mughals as they traveled from Delhi to Agra, a major seat of Mughal power, finally culminating in Kashmir". Brandon's team of seven (an Australian, two Canadians and four Americans), all history enthusiasts have concluded the Delhi leg. However, unlike last year, they will not be going to Kashmir this time to visit the Mughal Gardens, the pristine Dal Lake and other historic shrines. Instead, they will be off to Ladakh to interact with the locals and capture the rugged beauty there.

The workshops are conducted for a small group of people interested in photography and a cross-cultural experience. "For years nobody focused on understanding Muslim history. Often I meet people who have visited the Taj Mahal and have no clue about who built the monument. Most foreigners consider the Taj to be a Hindu shrine," he explains. Brandon is assisted by friend, David Du Chemin, 36, a Canadian photographer whose expertise lies in guiding aspiring photographers on how to achieve the perfect shot. "I believe that you can tell a compelling story in a single frame. So we teach the students how to make a picture visually powerful. We also like to introduce people to experiences that we have shared," says Chemin. Brandon also recently published a coffee table book about the Valley called Kashmir: The Mystery. The members of the workshop do not want to explore the city in its entirety for a simple reason, points out Chemin, "We know Old Delhi and Nizamuddin Dargah fairly well. There is so much vitality in Chandi Chowk. We would rather have a deep experience in one place."

For more details log on to www.lumen-dei.com

Heading: First ‘no jobs’, now students of UBS caught in litigation web - Indian Express
Content:
There seems to be no end to the problems faced by the Central Bureau of Investigation in the cash-at-judge's-door case. Despite arresting all the accused, including Delhi-based hotelier Ravinder Singh, the investigation agency is still groping in the dark to unearth the actual motive behind the scam.

With Ravinder Singh denying his involvement in the cash transaction, the CBI is yet to ascertain the motive.

Ravinder Singh surrendered before the Special Court of CBI Judge Jagdeep Jain on Friday and revealed that the packet containing Rs 15 lakh in cash, which was "wrongly delivered" at the residence of Justice Nirmaljit Kaur, did not belong to him.

Sources in CBI said Ravinder Singh is proving to be a tough nut as he has flatly denied any involvement in the case and was not cooperating in the case.

"It appears that he has been briefed by his well-wishers. He has flatly denied any involvement in the case without giving any reasons. He knows that we cannot interrogate him beyond a certain limit and he is just taking advantage of this fact," said a CBI officer.

Sources said the investigating agency is also exploring the possibility of any pending judicial case, for which the money could have been sent through Sanjeev Bansal. Although, the CBI has shortlisted a few cases pending in the Punjab and Haryana High Court, it has not been able to find out any specific case to attribute the bribe.

Moreover, the deadlock regarding the place, where the two women judges of the High Court will be examined, is yet to be decided. The CBI has taken a clear stand that the two judges cannot be examined at their residence.

Sources added that a team of CBI officers from Delhi has also met Chief Justice Tirath Singh Thakur more than twice in this regard. The CBI has requested that the two judges should be asked to come either to their zonal office or any other place but not their residence.

"The judges cannot be examined at their residence. During the time of questioning, the conduct of a person is observed. We can't carry all the documents and ask the entire team to come to someone's residence for examination. The very purpose of examination will stand defeated if they have to be questioned at their residence. Moreover, all witnesses have come to the CBI office.

If the judges are examined at their residence, then other accused and witnesses might object to it. We have met the Chief Justice in this regard and he has assured us that he will intimate us after speaking to the two Judges," said another CBI sleuth.

However, examining the two judges will now take a backseat till the time CBI completes the custodial interrogation of Ravinder Singh. Sources added that no questionnaire will be sent by the CBI to the two Judges for examination. "We have drafted some questions, which the judges will be asked to answer. In order to take the investigation ahead, we need to examine the two Judges personally and not by the mode of any questionnaire," said a CBI official.

Heading: Eviction: Jhota Kut Colony razed - Indian Express
Content:
It has been nearly a month since the job placements for students at the University Business School, Panjab University, was held up following a petition filed by the management students at the PU regional centre, Ludhiana. The students have suffered another jolt with legal experts suggesting that the lawyer hired by these students to represent their side cannot interfere in the case going on in the High Court. Consequently, nearly Rs 1 lakh paid by the students to the lawyer has also apparently gone down the drain.

The management students at the PU regional centre at Ludhiana had recently filed a case against the Panjab University demanding to hold their placements along with the students at UBS Chandigarh. While the case was still pending in the court, the authorities at the department were misinformed that the placements of the students of UBS Chandigarh had been stayed as a result of which, the placements were halted for the students.

Without cross checking, the department halted the placement procedure and instructed its students to stop communicating with companies regarding job placements till the said case was resolved.

Chairperson, UBS, Dinesh Gupta said, "We have been advised by our varsity counsel to halt the proceedings and that is what we have done".

Clarifying his stand Anupam Gupta, UT Counsel, said, "We are doing what we can and it is out of the technicalities involved that I have advised the department to halt the placement procedure. Students need not worry as we will do our best for them".

Looking for a solution, the panic-stricken students approached a city-based lawyer, Sanjeev Walia, who was incidentally the father of their batchmate, Sangam Walia.

Talking to Newsline, one of the students from the department said, "We were worried after students from Ludhiana filed a writ petition and our placements were stopped. Sangam told us that his father was ready to fight our side but would charge Rs 1,50,000."

After negotiations, the deal was settled at around Rs 1 lakh with the 150 students paying Rs 700 each.

Asked to comment on whether he could interfere in the case, Walia said, "It's after the students approached me that I decided to take up their case and they paid the fee on their own. I have made these students a party to the case and shall be fighting their case".

On meeting the vice-chancellor on Friday, the students were politely refused any help and were told that the matter would be dealt with by Dean University Instructions (DUI).

The Court had earlier issued a notice to the University and directed it to file its reply on September 18. With the University failing to reply, the case was adjourned to September 25.

Heading: UT announces awards for Teachers’ Day function - Indian Express
Content:
One of the oldest slums in Mohali — Jhota Kut Colony in Sector 71 — was pulled down in a major eviction drive carried out by the Greater Mohali Area Development Authority (GMADA) on Saturday evening.

GMADA vacated almost five acres of prime land worth several crores in the heart of the city, which was encroached upon since 1980s. While almost 100 concrete structures were razed in today's anti-encroachment drive, the occupants of the remaining 300 structures were given a day's time to move out otherwise they will also be removed forcibly, GMADA officials said.

With this, hundreds of residents of Sector 71, 70, 3B2 and industrial area in the vicinity heaved a sigh of relief.

GMADA will carve out around 50 plots measuring one kanal and 16 marlas each, besides developing a park in continuity with the development of Sector 71 in the vacated land.

"We were able to act after winning the legal battle that continued for years," GMADA Chief Administrator Vivek Partap Singh told Newsline.

On September 17, a Punjab and Haryana High Court division bench, comprising Chief Justice Tirath Singh Thakur and Justice Surya Kant, had "dismissed on merit" a latter patent appeal (LPA) filed by R S Sandhu and others against the dispossession of the colony dwellers.

GMADA Estate Officer (EO) Sukhjeet Pal Singh said that the land was acquired in the 1970s for the development of Sector 71 but in the 1980s, Jhota Kut Colony surfaced on it "illegally".

"When efforts were made to remove the encroachment, the colony dwellers moved courts and procured stay on their dispossession, which continued till last year," said Pal Singh.

He said that after the stay was vacated, the colony dwellers filed an LPA before the High Court, which finally on Wednesday ordered them to vacate it.

Around 100 enforcement wing employees of GMADA, led by two Sub-Divisional Officers (SDOs) S K Bains and Surinder Singh, with the help of bulldozers and almost 30 police personnel swooped on the colony around 1.30 pm and demolished almost 90 commercial and 10 residential structures till 5.30 pm.

"Due to rain, the squatters sought time to move out voluntarily, following which we asked them to vacate till tomorrow," said Pal Singh, while adding that the drive will continue till the area is cleared of encroachment.

He confirmed that since the colony dwellers were aware of having no legal right over the land under their possession, nobody resisted the drive and instead started shifting their belongings from the illegal structures.

Pal Singh said some portion of the vacated land will be used in the ongoing project of widening the roads passing through the area.

Mohali Citizens' Welfare Federation president B S Tej has welcomed the action. "Residents in the vicinity got rid of slum and filth,

|which has been making their lives hell since years," said Tej, while demanding immediate development of the vacated land to avoid resurfacing of the encroachment.

Kharar MLA Balbir Sidhu also lauded the drive but demanded rehabilitation of the displaced dwellers.

"A separate colony on the same lines of Milk Colony in Dhanas is needed in Mohali to shift all dairies and slums from different parts of the city," he demanded.

Heading: Auto ban: Hunt on for transport as Admn provides no options - Indian Express
Content:
The UT Education Department today announced the names of 12 teachers who will be conferred national and state awards at the Teachers' Day function on September 22.

Pritpal Kaur, Mission Co-ordinator of the Sarv Shiksha Abhiyan, will be presented the lifetime achievement award. Pritpal has worked for the mission for over three decades.

There are be two national awardees and nine state awardees this year. Dharam Pal Sharma, TGI Sanskrit (GMHS-37 C), and Jasmine P Jakhar, Lecturer (GMSSS-35 C), have been named for the national awards.

The state awardees include: Manoj Kumar Sharda, Lecturer (GMSSS-8B); Dr Anil K Gugnani, Lecturer (SIE-32); Preeti Garg, Lecturer (GMSSS-10); Rita Batra, Headmistress (GMHS-36); Sweety Behl, Lecturer (DAV Model School-15); Pushpa Rani, music teacher (GHS-24); Dalvinder Kaur, NTT (GMHS-41); Gyan Chand, S S Master (GMHS-41); Narinder Shastri, Sanskrit teacher (GHS Mouli Colony).

Sweety Behl is the first teacher from the various DAV schools of Chandigarh to be honoured with the prestigious award. Principal of DAV Model School, Sector 15, Rakesh Sachdeva said: "It is a moment of great pride for the school."

"Sweety Behl completed her MSc from Government Home Science College, Sector 10, and MEd from Maharishi Dayanand University, Rohtak. In 1990, she joined DAV Model School as lecturer of Home Science. She is also serving as incharge of Certificate in Education Institute of DAV," said a spokesperson.

Heading: PU scholar raises doubts on credibility of forthcoming Senate elections - Indian Express
Content:
Come January and government school students shall have to face a tough time commuting to school and back, courtesy the UT Administration. The authorities have banned auto-rickshaws from ferrying students, however at the same time have arranged for no other alternative. The schools have been directed to arrange for an alternative on their own.

In a recent decision, the Chandigarh Administration had decided to ban auto-rickshaws from ferrying students.

The decision, however, has created a feeling of unrest among both parents as well as students since no alternative has been suggested except that the students can travel in 'vehicles covered from all sides'.

Talking to Newsline, Education-cum-Finance Secretary Sanjay Kumar said, "The decision has been taken keeping in mind the safety of the students. The schools can tie up with private players on their own and arrange for alternative modes of conveyance for the students."

The decision has evoked much criticism from the schools, who have taken it as an additional responsibility. One government school principal said, "After the Administration announced a ban on auto-rickshaws, we have many parents approaching us with suitable alternatives. Arranging transport has come as an additional burden and to look for vehicles covered from four sides to ferry students is not an easy task." It is the parents, meanwhile who are the most harassed lot since they cannot seem to find any other option. A few parents are afraid that the schools do not have a binding to arrange for transport and can also deny the same.

Ashok Kumar, a parent of a Class III student in Government Model Senior Secondary School, Sector 18, said: "We had no issues arranging for autos but after the ban it would be difficult for us to arrange for vehicles covered from all four sides. We have decided to meet senior officials to discuss the issue."

Officials from the department, on the other hand, have also welcomed private players interested in tying up with the department to arrange for transportation.

Heading: De-addiction centre owner held - Indian Express
Content:
A Fellow in the Department Of Evening Studies, PU, and also a prominent candidate from the graduates' constituency for the PU Senate, has alleged grave injustice in having the DAV institutions as election booths for the senate elections on Sunday.

The reason cited by Fellow Dr Rabindra Nath Sharma — the DAV connection of the candidates with M L Aeri being the Director, Colleges of the DAV Colleges Managing Committee, New Delhi, and Principal Kackria and Principal Kaul, working as principals in DAV Colleges.

In a complaint to Prof R C Sobti, Vice-Chancellor, Panjab University, the complainant added that not only are these candidates using the money and manpower resources of the DAV Colleges Managing Committee, New Delhi to get themselves elected, but with DAV Institutions as election booths for the Senate elections, the need for having impartial and neutral venues has been overlooked by the University.

"It is surprising that with various government and private schools and colleges available across the street, the DAV institutions have been selected as polling booths.

In Chandigarh, DAV College, Section 10, and DAV Schools of Sectors 8 and 15 are polling stations despite other institutions present in their vicinity."

Sharma alleged that on Election Day, the staff

of these schools and colleges has been deputed to work for Aeri and others and the voters are likely to be swayed in favour of them.

He urged the authorities to either shift the polling booths immediately, or appoint observers to ensure that polling is conducted in a fair and unbiased manner.

13 from Ludhiana in race for PU Senate

The fate of thirteen candidates from the district, who are in the fray for three different constituencies - graduates, principals and lecturers - in the fourth phase of Panjab University Senate elections, is going to be sealed in the ballot boxes on Sunday. Over two lakh voters are expected to exercise their franchise to elect the senators of the PU Senate in the elections being held in various affiliated colleges of the university today.

While Praveen Sharma, Rajiv Bhasin, Jagpal Singh, Lakhvinder Singh Bedi and Madanjit Kaur Sahota are contesting in the graduates' constituency from the district, the principals constituency includes Dr Satish Sharma, Dr Varinder Kaur Thind, Dr Narinder Singh Sidhu, Dr RS Jhanji and Dr Rekha Bhardwaj from the district. The lecturer constituency has Mukesh Arora, Harpreet Dua and Kuldeep Singh in the fray.

"I am quite hopeful of winning the elections. Though I have not sent a single letter to the voters seeking their support or spent any extra money on the campaign, except for phone calls, I am still sure that I will win with a huge margin," said Prof Mukesh Arora, of SCD Government College who is also a three-time winner in the senate elections.

"I have tried to live up to the expectations of the voters who voted me to be the youngest senator in the house last time and therefore I am hopeful of winning this time around too," was how Harpreet Dua summed up his chances of being a senator again.

On the other hand, a principal constituency candidate Dr Varinder Kaur Thind, principal of Khalsa College for Women, who is contesting the elections for the first time, said, "As it all depends upon one's personal relations, I am positive about

winning," she beamed.

There are 42 candidates - five of them from Ludhiana - vying for 15 seats in the largest graduates' constituency wherein over two lakh voters are expected to cast their vote. There are about 4.15 lakh registered voters in the constituency.

In the lecturers' constituency, out of the total of 12 candidates who are in the fray, three are from the district. They are contesting for eight seats to be voted for by 2200 voters.

The principals' constituency has 13 principals contesting for eight seats. There are five candidates from the district alone in the constituency with an electorate strength of 70.

Heading: Rahul Gandhi to address Congress workers on Monday - Indian Express
Content:
3 days after he was admitted in de-addiction centre, Sonu was found dead outside his house

Kharar police on Saturday arrested one of the owners of a drug de-addiction centre in Balongi village a month after a taxi driver's body was found dumped in his house's courtyard after he was admitted in the centre for treatment.

The taxi driver, Surinder Singh, alias Sonu, had been admitted in Sankalp, a drug de-addiction centre in Balongi village, on August 21 for treatment. Three days later, his body was reportedly dumped in his courtyard in the early hours by some of the centre's workers, following which, the owner and staffers of the centre were booked on charges of torturing him.

Kharar Station House Officer (SHO) Dalbeer Singh, who was the investigating officer, had registered an FIR under sections 304 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder), 148 (rioting armed with deadly weapon) and 149 (unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object) of the Indian Penal Code against Ramanjot Singh alias Goldy.

Later, he was remanded in two-day judicial custody by a local court on Saturday.

Police said Goldy was one of the owners of the centre and was believed to be the main accused who tortured Sonu to death.

"We are hoping to lay hands on other offenders after we interrogate Goldy," said Dalbeer Singh.

An FIR was lodged after Sonu's roommate Kamaljeet Singh registered his statement with the police.

He said that Sonu was admitted in the centre on August 21 and next day, when he complained of pain in his leg, in which an iron rod was implanted earlier, the officials on duty took him to a private hospital in Phase IV. There the doctors reportedly ruled out any kind of complication and released him. Sonu tried to escape but the centre officials managed to keep hold of him.

On bringing him back to the centre on Friday, Kamaljeet said that the centre owner and staffers subjected Sonu to third-degree torture, following which he fell unconscious. On August 22, Sonu was taken away from the centre when he was unconscious.

Kamaljeet claimed that the centre owner and staffers were panic stricken as Sonu had died, therefore they dumped him at his house and fled away.

Following which, Sonu's family members and relatives held demonstration on August 23 and blocked vehicular traffic on the busy Mohali-Kharar stretch of NH-21.

They even accused the police of "shielding" the owner and staffers of Sankalp drug de-addiction centre in Balongi and said that Sonu was "tortured" to death while he was getting treated.

There are over 34 de-addiction centres in Punjab, but most do not have a permanent psychiatrist and warden. Blatant human rights violations have also been recorded in the past.

Heading: Youth washed away by heavy currents of Markanda - Indian Express
Content:
On his maiden visit to Punjab, the All India Congress Committee (AICC) general secretary Rahul Gandhi is all set to visit Chandigarh, Mohali on Monday. During his visit, he will be addressing the Congress members as well as the Youth Congress.

After landing at the airport at 10 am, he will move towards Hallomajra and will interact with the residents. Kharar MLA Balbir Sidhu today told Newsline that Rahul will reach Dussehra Ground in Phase VIII around 11 am to inspect the progress of ongoing membership drive of the Youth Congress besides interacting with the party leaders, workers and residents gathered on the spot.

Following which, Rahul will join a roadshow to Kharar via Sohana and Landran and reach Morinda, where he will be again interact with the Youth Congress members there. From Morinda, Rahul will move to Fatehgarh Sahib and reach Patiala for a night stay.

Heading: Waterlogging, parking woes ail Sector 16 - Indian Express
Content: A youth, working with a factory at Rasaur village near Naraingarh drowned in the River Markanda on Saturday morning. The deceased, identified as one Narinder Kumar, and his associate were on their way to the factory when they were washed away by the currents. While his associate managed to reach the shore, Narinder died. The dead body has been sent for postmortem in civil hospital in Naraingarh.

Heading: Hopefully, better things lie ahead for me this year: Pujara - Indian Express
Content:
As the residents of Sector 16 list their complaints, two common problems come to the fore — waterlogging and parking woes.

The heavy rainfall that pelted the city recently has intensified the problem leaving the low-lying areas inundated with water.

Samvadini, a resident of the sector says, "The problem of waterlogging is acute in our sector. The slightest of rainfall can cause blockage in some areas. There needs to be an improvement in the sewerage system to prevent the problem. We had to face a tough time during the rains."

With a government school present in the sector, there is a constant struggle for parking as students who do not have valid licences to park their vehicles in the nearby market.

Mohit, a resident, says, "There is little space for parking and several times the vehicles can be seen lined up on the road. Proper planning is the need of the hour."

Pointing out the presence of a liquor shop in the area, Mohit adds, "It should be closed as a liquor shop should not be present in close proximity of the school." While urging for better upkeep of the parks, the residents asked for clearance of overgrown grass and waste construction material. Despite a fine imposed for dumping waste, scant regard is being paid to it.

Area councillor Mayor Pardeep Chhabra, however, maintained that development plans for the sector are on the anvil. "The parks are being taken care of and after the monsoons end, these would be spruced up. The recarpetting of roads would also be done," he added.

He also added: "Paver blocks are being laid in different parts of the sector. A Sehaj Safai Kendra has been approved for the sector. This will deal with the problem of dumping of garbage. Swings and benches are being installed in various parks. While work has already been done at some places, it would be completed in the coming days. Beautification of Shanti Kunj is going on. Work is also being done through MPLAD funds."

Heading: Sushil felicitated at akhara - Indian Express
Content:
With two back to back centuries in Buchi Babu cricket tournament, Cheteshwar Pujara has reinstated that he is hungry for more in the coming Ranji season. Currently in Chandigarh to participate in the J P Atray tournament which he describes as 'decision of his team-mates and the company', he says he is looking forward to repeat his last year's performance in the Ranji Trophy.
